 25    - title: How to use JSF 1.2 with EAP 7?
 26      url: https://access.redhat.com/solutions/2773121
 27    message: "\n                        Seam 2.2 and earlier is not supported on JBoss
 28      EAP 6 and above.\n                        Consider migration to Context Dependency
 29      Injection (CDI) standard which covers most of Seam 2 core functionalities in\n
 30      \                       a standardized, type safe and extensible way.\n                        \n
 31      \                       Seam 2.3 still could work on EAP 6.x, but is not maintained
 32      and officially supported on new EAP 6.x patched releases or EAP 7.x.\n\n                        There
 33      are two options available:\n                        \n                        1.
 34      Continue using Seam 2.x on EAP 6 but expect there are bugs or glitches and you
 35      need to fix it yourself.\n                        This approach is sometimes lower
 36      effort but the application will not use a tested and supported library and some
 37      Seam framework features doesn't have to work as expected.\n                        2.
 38      The similar approach as for point 1 but for Seam 2.3 runtime on EAP7 is not verified
 39      and therefore not recommended. Some Seam 2.3 features could work on EAP7,\n                        but
 40      the expected behavior can differ based on what your application uses and how.\n
 41      \                       2. Switch to standard CDI beans and migrate to JSF 2.2
 42      if your server platform is EAP 7+. This will require significant migration effort.\n
 43      \                   "

 20      This is a JDBC URL, which describes the basic information about
 21       where and how to connect to the database.
 22       This particular URL points to a PostgreSQL database.
 23  
 24       In EAP 6, the databases are configured in these steps:
 25  
 26       1. Add the JDBC driver as an EAP 6 module. Download it [here](https://jdbc.postgresql.org/download.html).
 27       2. Create a datasource (actual values need to be changed):
 28       ```
 29       $ EAP_HOME/bin/jboss-cli --connect
 30       [standalone@localhost:9999 /] data-source add --name=ExampleDS --jndi-name=java:/ExampleDS \\
 31       --connection-url=... --driver-name=postgresql \\
 32       --user-name=... --password=...
 33       ```
 34       3. Use the datasource according to JPA 2.0 standards.

 987    links: []
 988    message: |-
 989      Previous versions of Hibernate have mapped `byte[]` and `Byte[]` to Oracle’s `LONG RAW` data type (via the JDBC `LONGVARBINARY` type). Oracle have deprecated the `LONG RAW` data type for many releases - possibly as far back as 8i.
 990  
 991       Therefore it was decided to start having Hibernate map `byte[]` and `Byte[]` to `BLOB` for Oracle.
 992  
 993       However, in the interest of backwards compatibility and not breaking existing applications it was also decided to limit this change to just the `Oracle12cDialect`. So starting in 5.1 applications using `Oracle12cDialect` and implicitly mapping `byte[]` and `Byte[]` values will start seeing those handled as `BLOB` data rather than `LONG RAW` data.
 994       For existing applications that want to continue to use `Oracle12cDialect` and still continue to implicitly map `byte[]` and `Byte[]` attributes to `LONG RAW`, there is a new configuration setting you can use to enable that: `hibernate.dialect.oracle.prefer_longvarbinary`, which is `false `by default (map to `BLOB`).

 45    message: |-
 46      Replace class `org.jboss.resteasy.client.ClientRequest` with `org.jboss.resteasy.client.jaxrs.ResteasyClient`.
 47  
 48       The following is an example of how to send a link header with the RESTEasy client in EAP 6 with RESTEasy 2.3.x.
 49  
 50       ```java
 51       ClientRequest request = new ClientRequest(generateURL("/linkheader/str"));
 52       request.addLink("previous chapter", "previous", "http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2", null);
 53       ClientResponse response = request.post();
 54       LinkHeader header = response.getLinkHeader();
 55       ```
 56  
 57       The following is an example of how to accomplish the same task with the RESTEasy client in RESTEasy 3.
 58  
 59       ```java
 60       ResteasyClient client = new ResteasyClientBuilder().build();
 61       Response response = client.target(generateURL("/linkheader/str")).request()
 62       .header("Link", "<http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2>; rel="previous";
 63       title="previous chapter">").post(Entity.text(new String()));
 64       javax.ws.rs.core.Link link = response.getLink("previous");
 65       ```

 76      url: https://access.redhat.com/articles/1326823
 77    message: |-
 78      The WebLogic `<delay-updates-until-end-of-tx>` configuration element, which defaults to `true`, is used for performance reasons to delay updates to the persistent store of all beans until the end of the transaction. When set to `false`, updates are sent to the database after each method invocation, but are not committed until the end of the transaction. This allows other processes to access the persisted data while the transaction is waiting to be completed.
 79  
 80       In JBoss EAP 6+, you can achieve the same behavior by specifying the `<sync-on-commit-only>` in the jbosscmp-jdbc.xml file.

 37    message: |-
 38      Sonic ESB services leverage the service(XQServiceContext context) method to implement business logic. When messages are routed to the service, the service(XQServiceContext context) method is executed.
 39       In Camel, this is achieved by routing messages to the Java Bean via the Camel Route's Bean Component syntax.
 40  
 41       * [Camel Java Bean Component](http://camel.apache.org/bean.html)
 42       * [Camel Binding Annotations](http://camel.apache.org/parameter-binding-annotations.html)
 43  
 44       Camel's Java Bean Component can leverage annotations annotations on the method to specify how Camel Message body values are mapped to the method parameters. Additionally, the @Handler annotation can be leveraged to setup the default Java Bean method.
 45  
 46       **For example:**
 47  
 48       ```java
 49       public void service(XQServiceContext ctx) throws XQServiceException \{{
 50       ...
 51       }}
 52       ```
 53  
 54       **Should become:**
 55  
 56       ```java
 57       @Handler
 58       public void service(@Header messageHeader, @Body messageBody, Exchange exchange) \{{
 59       ...
 60       }}
 61       ```

 64       * org.apache.camel.Header
 65       * org.apache.camel.Exchange

653    message: |-
654      JBoss ESB uses notifiers to transform ESB aware messages to a format that ESB-unaware services can handle. Fuse Service Works uses bi-directional gateways to transfer messages
655       via its service bindings.
656  
657       A JBoss ESB Notifier should be converted to a Fuse Service Works Service Binding.
658  
659       For example:
660  
661       ```xml
662       <service category="routerToFile" name="FileRouterListener" description="Static route file destination">
663       <actions mep="OneWay">
664       <action name="notificationAction" class="org.jboss.soa.esb.actions.Notifier">
665       <property name="okMethod" value="notifyOK"/>
666       <property name="notification-details">
667       <NotificationList type="ok">
668       <target class="NotifyFiles">
669       <file append="false" URI="/tmp/HelloWorldFileNotifierTest.log"/>
670       </target>
671       </NotificationList>
672       </property>
673       </action>
674       </actions>
675       </service>
676       ```
677  
678  
679       Could be translated to:
680  
681       ```xml
682       <sca:reference name="HelloWorld" multiplicity="0..1" promote="MyComponent/HelloWorld">
683       <camel:binding.file>
684       <camel:directory>/tmp</camel:directory>
685       <camel:fileName>HelloWorldFileNotifierTest.log</camel:fileName>
686       </camel:binding.file>
687       </sca:reference>
688       <sca:component name="MyComponent">
689       <sca:reference name="HelloWorld">
690       <sca:interface.wsdl interface="HelloWorld.wsdl#wsdl.porttype(HelloWorld)"/>
691       </sca:reference>
692       </sca:component>
693       ```
694    ruleID: soa-p-31000
695    when:
696      builtin.xml:

Entity Enterprise JavaBeans 157 (EJB) \n

This rule flags entity elements in ejb-jar.xml 158 files.

\n

Entity beans are optional in the EJB 3.2 specification and 159 are not supported on Liberty or Liberty Core. The entity bean API is deprecated 160 in WebSphere Application Server traditional V8.5.5 and V9.0 and might be removed 161 in a later version.

\n

The EJBDeploy tool used to deploy applications 162 with entity beans has also been deprecated and may be removed in the future, either 163 at the same time entity beans are removed or prior.

\n

The Java Persistence 164 API (JPA) is an alternative to using EJB entity beans for new database and other 165 persistence-related operations.

\n

Upgrading entity beans can be difficult, 166 but it can be simplified if your application uses design patterns such as DTO, 167 Session Facade, and DAO.

\n
" 168 ruleID: DetectEJBEntityBeansXML 169 when: 170 builtin.xml: 171 filepaths: 172 - ejb-jar.xml 173 namespaces: {} 174 xpath: //*[local-name()='entity'] 175 - category: mandatory 176 customVariables: [] 177 description: Transaction propagation is not supported for Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB) 178 remote interfaces 179 effort: 1 180 labels: 181 - source=websphere 182 - target=openliberty 183 links: 184 - title: Open Liberty migration rules in Windup 185 url: https://www.ibm.com/docs/wamt?topic=rules-open-liberty-migration-in-windup 186 message: "
\n

Liberty does not support outbound or inbound 187 transaction propagation for EJB remote interfaces. By default, EJB beans are container-managed 188 and use the Required transaction attribute. As a result, existing 189 EJB definitions that do not specify any container-transaction properties 190 are configured by default to use transactions although they are not supported. 191

\n

This rule flags Java code that references the following EJB annotations 192 that indicate the use of remote business or home interfaces:

\n
    \n
  • javax.ejb.Remote
    • 193 \n
  • javax.ejb.RemoteHome
    • \n
\n

This rule also flags 194 the following references in the ejb-jar.xml file:

195 \n
    \n
  • <remote/>
    • \n
  • <business-remote/>
    • 196 \n
\n

The EJB specification requires products that support outbound 197 transaction propagation to still send a null transaction context. This context 198 must be rejected by EJB components that use the Required (default), 199 Mandatory , or Supports transaction attributes. A client 200 with an active global transaction cannot start an EJB bean with default transaction 201 attributes if either the client or server is on Liberty.

\n

To enable 202 the client to start the EJB bean, change the EJB bean to use either the RequiresNew 203 or NotSupported transaction attribute. Although these attributes 204 will allow the EJB bean to start, the transactional work that is done by the EJB 205 bean is not committed as part of the client transactions.

\n

Note that 206 transaction propagation is supported for EJB remote interfaces that are running 207 in the same JVM, however this may only be determined with further investigation 208 of the application behavior.

\n

Make sure remote EJB interfaces are needed

209 \n

Often EJB 2.x beans configure the remote interfaces in ejb-jar.xml even 210 when they are not used. You only need remote interfaces if you have code running 211 across two different JVMs. In WebSphere terms, this is either between two different 212 application servers or between a client application and an application server 213 running in different JVMs. CORBA information, such as an iiop:// 214 provider URL, in an EJB lookup is also an indicator that remote EJB beans are 215 being used.

\n

If you are referencing EJB beans using a remote interface 216 that are running in the same JVM, the Local interface can be used and will perform 217 better. Where possible, change annotations from @Remote to @Local and from @RemoteHome 218 to @LocalHome and test all your code scenarios. Likewise for ejb-jar.xml configuration, 219 remove the <remote/> and <business-remote/> 220 definitions and test all scenarios. While transaction propagation is supported 221 for this scenario, the best practice is to convert to using local interfaces to 222 improve performance and remove the perception that methods can be called externally 223 from the same JVM.

\n

If you really need remote interfaces

\n
Wrap 224 the EJB beans in a web service (JAX-WS)
\n

For those EJB beans that require 225 remote access, best practice is to wrap them in a web service. 1  - category: optional
  2    customVariables: []
  3    description: Move persistence config to a properties file
  4    effort: 1
  5    labels:
  6    - source=java-ee
  7    - source=jakarta-ee
  8    - target=quarkus
  9    links:
 10    - title: Using Hibernate ORM and Jakarta persistence
 11      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#persistence-xml
 12    message: "It is recommended to move persistence related configuration from an XML
 13      file to a properties one.\n This allows centralization of the configuration in
 14      Quarkus. Check the link for more information.\n \n \n Datasource and persistence
 15      configurations in XML can be substituted with a single centralized properties
 16      file. Here is an example of a translation:\n \n The following datasource configuration:\n
 17      ```\n <datasources xmlns=\"http://www.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema\"\n xmlns:xsi=\"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance\"\n
 18      xsi:schemaLocation=\"http://www.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema http://docs.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema/datasources_1_0.xsd\">\n
 19      <!-- The datasource is bound into JNDI at this location. We reference\n this in
 20      META-INF/persistence.xml -->\n <datasource jndi-name=\"java:jboss/datasources/TasksJsfQuickstartDS\"\n
 21      pool-name=\"tasks-jsf-quickstart\" enabled=\"true\"\n use-java-context=\"true\">\n
 22      <connection-url>jdbc:h2:mem:tasks-jsf-quickstart;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1</connection-url>\n
 23      <driver>h2</driver>\n <security>\n <user-name>sa</user-name>\n <password>sa</password>\n
 24      </security>\n </datasource>\n </datasources>\n ```\n along with the following
 25      persistence configuration:\n ```\n <persistence version=\"2.1\"\n xmlns=\"http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence\"
 26      xmlns:xsi=\"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance\"\n xsi:schemaLocation=\"\n
 27      http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence\n http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence/persistence_2_1.xsd\">\n
 28      <persistence-unit name=\"primary\">\n <!-- We use a different datasource for tests,
 29      so as to not overwrite\n production data. This is an unmanaged data source, backed
 30      by H2, an in memory\n database. Production applications should use a managed datasource.
 31      -->\n <!-- The datasource is deployed as WEB-INF/test-ds.xml,\n you can find it
 32      in the source at src/test/resources/test-ds.xml -->\n <jta-data-source>java:jboss/datasources/TasksJsfQuickstartDS</jta-data-source>\n
 33      <properties>\n <!-- Properties for Hibernate -->\n <property name=\"hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto\"
 34      value=\"create-drop\" />\n <property name=\"hibernate.show_sql\" value=\"false\"
 35      />\n </properties>\n </persistence-unit>\n </persistence>\n ```\n can be translated
 36      to:\n ```\n quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:tasks-jsf-quickstart;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1\n
 37      quarkus.datasource.db-kind=h2\n quarkus.datasource.username=sa\n quarkus.datasource.password=sa\n\n
 38      quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation=drop-and-create\n ```"
 39    ruleID: persistence-to-quarkus-00000
 40    when:
 41      or:
 42      - builtin.file:
 43          pattern: persistence\.xml
 44      - builtin.file:
 45          pattern: .*-ds\.xml

 48    description: '@Produces cannot annotate an EntityManager'
 49    effort: 1
 50    labels:
 51    - source=java-ee
 52    - source=jakarta-ee
 53    - target=quarkus
 54    links:
 55    - title: Using Hibernate ORM and Jakarta persistence
 56      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#persistence-xml
 57    - title: Setting up and configuring Hibernate ORM
 58      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#setting-up-and-configuring-hibernate-orm
 59    message: "In JavaEE/JakartaEE, using `@PersistenceContext` was needed in order to
 60      inject a data source. Quarkus, on the other hand,\n will create the bean automatically
 61      just by correctly setting up your datasource, so the `@PersistenceContext` annotation can be removed. \nThis also makes having a `@Produces`
 62      annotation\n on the `EntityManager` illegal in Quarkus.\n \n If you are using
 63      a `@Produces` annotation for your EntityManager, and it is not needed after configuring
 64      your datasource, remove it and `@Inject` the EntityManager.\n Otherwise, if the
 65      producer is still needed, please create a qualification for your produced `EntityManager`,
 66      as well as every injection point for the EM.\n \n For instance, you can create
 67      an `ExtendedContext` qualifier:\n ```\n @Qualifier\n @Target({{ ElementType.TYPE,
 68      ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.PARAMETER }})\n @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)\n
 69      public @interface ExtendedContext {{ ... }}\n ```\n and then inject your entity
 70      managers:\n ```\n @ExtendedContext\n public EntityManager getEm() {{\n return
 71      em;\n }}\n ```"
 72    ruleID: persistence-to-quarkus-00011
 73    when:
 74      and:

 76          location: IMPORT
 77          pattern: javax.enterprise.inject.Produces
 78        as: file
 79        ignore: true
 80      - java.referenced:
 81          location: IMPORT
 82          pattern: javax.persistence.EntityManager
 83        from: file

 87    description: Changes to the DDL type for CLOB
 88    message: |
 89      Using `@Lob` or `java.sql.Clob` with PostgreSQL 8.1 dialect might require DDL type changes for CLOBs.
 90  
 91      Consider reviewing DDL generation for CLOB columns and potential migration to 'oid' type if necessary.
 92  
 93      All PostgreSQL JDBC drivers unfortunately just store the oid it created for a `java.sql.Clob` into the text column. 
 94      Although reading back the value with the CLOB API works, PostgreSQL has no knowledge of the reference to the LOB, 
 95      because the oid is not known to PostgreSQL, leading to data loss when vacuumlo (the utility to clean up unused LOBs) runs. 
 96      To avoid the data loss, it is required to use the oid type so that vacuumlo can see the reference.
 97  
 98      Updating to 5.6.2 does not require any schema or application changes by default, but we highly recommend that you migrate 
 99      existing text columns for LOBs to oid to prevent data loss due to the activity of vacuumlo.

423        pattern: org.springframework.security.web.authentication.rememberme.TokenBasedRememberMeServices
424        location: IMPORT
425    description: Use SHA-256 in Remember Me
426    message: |
427      The `TokenBasedRememberMeServices` implementation now supports SHA-256 for the Remember Me token and this is the
428      default in Spring Security 6. This change makes the implementation more secure by default since MD5 is already proven
429      to be a weak hashing algorithm and vulnerable against collision attacks and modular differential attacks.
430    
431      The new generated tokens now have the information of which algorithm was used to generate the token and that information
432      is used in order to match it. If the algorithm name is not present, then the matchingAlgorithm property is used to check
433      the token. This allows for a smooth transition from MD5 to SHA-256.
434      
435      To opt into the new Spring Security 6 default to encode the tokens while still being able to decode tokens encoded with MD5,
436      you can set the encodingAlgorithm property to SHA-256 and the matchingAlgorithm property to MD5. See the reference
437      documentation and the API docs for more information.

443        url: https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/5.8/migration/servlet/authentication.html#servlet-opt-in-sha256-rememberme

500    description: Change the order value in @EnableTransactionManagement
501    message: |
502      `@EnableTransactionManagement` and `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity` have the same order value, `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. This means
503      that their order in the Spring AOP Advisor chain relative to each other is undefined.
504    
505      This is often fine since most method security expressions don’t require an open transaction to function correctly;
506      however, historically it was sometimes necessary to ensure one happens before the other by setting their order values.
507      
508      @EnableMethodSecurity does not have an order value since it publishes multiple interceptors. Indeed, it cannot
509      attempt backward-compatibility with @EnableTransactionManagement since it cannot set all the interceptors to be in the same advisor chain location.
510      
511      Instead, the values for the `@EnableMethodSecurity` interceptors are based off of an offset of 0. The `@PreFilter` interceptor
512      has an order of 100; `@PostAuthorize`, 200; and so on.
513  
514      So, if after updating you find that your method security expressions are not working due to not having an open
515      transaction, please change your transaction annotation definition from the following:

542    message: |
543      As a performance optimization, a new method was introduced to `MethodSecurityExpressionHandler` that takes a `Supplier<Authentication>` instead of an `Authentication`.
544      This allows Spring Security to defer the lookup of the `Authentication`, and is taken advantage of automatically when you use `@EnableMethodSecurity` instead of `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`.
545      
546      However, let’s say that your code extends DefaultMethodSecurityExpressionHandler and overrides
547      `createSecurityExpressionRoot(Authentication, MethodInvocation)` to return a custom `SecurityExpressionRoot` instance.
548      This will no longer work because the arrangement that `@EnableMethodSecurity` sets up calls `createEvaluationContext(Supplier<Authentication>, MethodInvocation)` instead.
549      
550      Happily, such a level of customization is often unnecessary. Instead, you can create a custom bean with the authorization methods that you need.
551  
552      For example, let’s say you are wanting a custom evaluation of `@PostAuthorize("hasAuthority('ADMIN')")`. You can create a custom `@Bean` like this one:
553      ```

555        boolean isAdmin(MethodSecurityExpressionOperations root) {
556          boolean decision = root.hasAuthority("ADMIN");
557          // custom work ...
558          return decision;
559        }
560      }
561      ```
562      and then refer to it in the annotation like so:
563      ```
564      @PreAuthorize("@authz.isAdmin(#root)")

 19    message: |-
 20      This is a JDBC URL, which describes the basic information about
 21       where and how to connect to the database.
 22       This particular URL points to a PostgreSQL database.
 23  
 24       In EAP 6, the databases are configured in these steps:
 25  
 26       1. Add the JDBC driver as an EAP 6 module. Download it [here](https://jdbc.postgresql.org/download.html).
 27       2. Create a datasource (actual values need to be changed):
 28       ```
 29       $ EAP_HOME/bin/jboss-cli --connect
 30       [standalone@localhost:9999 /] data-source add --name=ExampleDS --jndi-name=java:/ExampleDS \\
 31       --connection-url=... --driver-name=postgresql \\
 32       --user-name=... --password=...
 33       ```
 34       3. Use the datasource according to JPA 2.0 standards.

 17      Default Remote JNDI Provider URL has changed in EAP 7. External applications using JNDI to lookup remote resources, for instance an EJB or a JMS Queue,
 18       may need to change the value for the JNDI InitialContext environment's property named `java.naming.provider.url`.
 19       The default URL scheme is now **http-remoting** instead of **remote**, and the default URL port is now **8080** instead of **4447**.
 20  
 21       As an example, consider the application server host is localhost, then clients previously accessing EAP 6 would use
 22  
 23       ```
 24       java.naming.factory.initial=org.jboss.naming.remote.client.InitialContextFactory
 25       java.naming.provider.url=remote://localhost:4447
 26       ```
 27  
 28       while clients now accessing EAP 7 should use instead
 29  
 30       ```
 31       java.naming.factory.initial=org.jboss.naming.remote.client.InitialContextFactory
 32       java.naming.provider.url=http-remoting://localhost:8080
 33       ```

690    category: mandatory

697    when:
698      java.referenced:
699        pattern: org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity.authorizeRequests
700        location: METHOD_CALL
701    description: Ensure that all requests have defined authorization rules
702    message: |
703      In Spring Security 5.8 and earlier, requests with no authorization rule are permitted by default. It is a stronger
704      security position to deny by default, thus requiring that authorization rules be clearly defined for every endpoint.
705      As such, in 6.0, Spring Security by default denies any request that is missing an authorization rule.
706      
707      The simplest way to prepare for this change is to introduce an appropriate `anyRequest` rule as the last authorization rule.
708      The recommendation is `denyAll` since that is the implied 6.0 default.
709      
710      Adding `denyAll` to the end looks like changing:
711      ```
712      http
713      .authorizeRequests((authorize) -> authorize
714          .filterSecurityInterceptorOncePerRequest(true)
715          .mvcMatchers("/app/**").hasRole("APP")
716          // ...
717      )
718      // ...
719      ```
720      to:
721      ```
722      http
723      .authorizeRequests((authorize) -> authorize
724          .filterSecurityInterceptorOncePerRequest(true)
725          .mvcMatchers("/app/**").hasRole("APP")
726          // ...
727          .anyRequest().denyAll()
728      )
729      // ...
730      ```
731

749    description: Migrate hasIpAddress to access(AuthorizationManager)
750    message: |
751      `hasIpAddress` has no DSL equivalent in `authorizeHttpRequests`. As such, you need to change any calls to `hasIpAddress` to using an `AuthorizationManager`.
752      
753      First, construct an IpAddressMatcher like so:
754      ```
755      IpAddressMatcher hasIpAddress = new IpAddressMatcher("127.0.0.1");
756      ```
757      and then change from this:
758      ```
759      http
760      .authorizeRequests((authorize) -> authorize
761          .mvcMatchers("/app/**").access("hasIpAddress('127.0.0.1')")
762          .anyRequest().denyAll()
763      )
764      // ...
765      ```
766      to this:
767      ```
768      http
769      .authorizeHttpRequests((authorize) -> authorize
770          .requestMatchers("/app/**").access((authentication, context) ->
771              new AuthorizationDecision(hasIpAddress.matches(context.getRequest()))
772          // ...
773          .anyRequest().denyAll()
774      )
775      // ...
776      ```

796  #      TODO: weak rule. The patterns above does not seem to work, so had to simplify it.
797        pattern: access(String)
798        location: METHOD_CALL
799    description: Migrate SpEL expressions to AuthorizationManager
800    message: |
801      For authorization rules, Java tends to be easier to test and maintain than SpEL. As such, authorizeHttpRequests
802      does not have a method for declaring a String SpEL. Instead, you can implement your own AuthorizationManager
803      implementation or use WebExpressionAuthorizationManager.
804  
805      If you have the following SpEL:
806      ```
807      http
808      .authorizeRequests((authorize) -> authorize
809          .filterSecurityInterceptorOncePerRequest(true)
810          .mvcMatchers("/complicated/**").access("hasRole('ADMIN') || hasAuthority('SCOPE_read')")
811          // ...
812          .anyRequest().denyAll()
813      )
814      // ...
815      ```
816      you can compose your own AuthorizationManager with Spring Security authorization primitives like so:
817      ```
818      http
819      .authorizeHttpRequests((authorize) -> authorize
820          .shouldFilterAllDispatcherTypes(false)
821          .mvcMatchers("/complicated/**").access(anyOf(hasRole("ADMIN"), hasAuthority("SCOPE_read"))
822          // ...
823          .anyRequest().denyAll()
824      )
825      // ...
826      ```

276    message: |-
277      To migrate a Java application that uses a MongoDB database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:
278  
279       * Use a managed **Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB**: Create a managed Cosmos DB for MongoDB database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements for performance, storage, and availability.
280  
281       * **Migrate your MongoDB data**: Take a backup of your MongoDB data and restore the backup to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB. You can use Azure Database Migration Service to facilitate the backup and restore process.
282  
283       * Update the application's **database connection** details: Modify your Java application's configuration to point to the new Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB instance. Update the connection string and authentication details in your application code to ensure connectivity to Azure Cosmos DB.
284  
285       * Enable **monitoring and diagnostics**: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.
286  
287       * Implement **security** measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.
288  
289       * **Backup** your data: Azure Cosmos DB provides built-in backup functionality that allows you to create automated backups of your data. Enable backup for your Azure Cosmos DB account and configure the backup retention policy to specify how long the backups should be retained.

Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.
389  
390       * **Use migration tools**: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.
391  
392       * **Update database drivers and connection strings**: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).
393  
394       * **Review and convert Oracle-specific code**: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.
395

397

This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.
399  
400       * **Backup** your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

 95      url: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/postgresql/single-server/concepts-backup
 96    message: |-
 97      To migrate a Java application that uses a PostgreSQL database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:
 98  
 99       * Use a managed **Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server**: For that create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements for performance, storage, and availability.
100  
101       * **Migrate** the existing PostgreSQL database: For that you can use the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) to perform an online migration with minimal downtime.
102  
103       * Update the application's **database connection** details: Modify the Java application's configuration to point to the newly provisioned Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Update the connection string, hostname, port, username, and password information accordingly.
104  
105       * Enable **monitoring and diagnostics**: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.
106  
107       * Implement **security** measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.
108  
109       * **Backup** your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

385    message: |-
386      Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:
387  
388       * **Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL**: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.
389  
390       * **Use migration tools**: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.
391  
392       * **Update database drivers and connection strings**: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).
393  
394       * **Review and convert Oracle-specific code**: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.
395  
396       * Enable **monitoring and diagnostics**: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.
397  
398       * Implement **security** measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.
399  
400       * **Backup** your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

458    message: |-
459      To migrate a Java application that uses a database to Azure, we recommend reviewing your architecture for cloud readiness and resilience. 
460      The following best practices will help improve reliability and avoid common pitfalls:
461  
462      * **Review and configure all timeout settings** (e.g., connection, socket, and transaction timeouts) based on real-world load and runtime behavior. Avoid hardcoding fixed values without load testing or telemetry.
463      * **Avoid infinite or excessively long timeouts.** Instead, favor "fail fast" patterns with proper error handling and retries where appropriate.
464      * **Lower default transaction timeouts,** especially for frameworks using JTA or other global transaction coordinators, to prevent long blocking under failure or overload conditions.
465      * **Implement exponential backoff** in client retry logic instead of fixed retry intervals. This helps reduce pressure on the system during partial outages and speeds up recovery by minimizing cascading retry storms.
466      * **Do not assume the database will always be available.** Cloud environments are inherently distributed and failure-prone. Design your application for transient failures, throttling, and restarts.
467  
468      Consider re-evaluating assumptions in your database interaction layer to ensure your application behaves reliably under cloud-native environments.

309       The old and new applications must be running on the same server or cluster. The new version of the application accepts new web session requests while the older version finishes processing requests already in process. Upon completion of the existing session requests, the older version of the application is then undeployed.
310  
311       In JBoss EAP, you can either deploy the new application to a secondary server group or cluster, or deploy the new application serially to the same clustered domain.

 54    links:
 55    - title: Azure Container Registry documentation
 56      url: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/
 57    - title: Migrate from Google Container Registry to Azure Container Registry
 58      url: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-import-images
 59    - title: Azure Container Registry best practices
 60      url: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-best-practices
 61    message: |-
 62      The application uses Google Container Registry (gcr.io) or Google Artifact Registry ([location]-docker.pkg.dev) for container images.
 63  
 64      **Common patterns detected may include:**
 65      * Container image references in Dockerfiles and docker-compose files
 66      * Kubernetes manifests (Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs, Pods) with GCR images
 67      * Configuration files referencing GCR endpoints
 68  
 69      **To migrate to Azure Container Registry (ACR):**
 70      * **Provision Azure Container Registry:**
 71         * Create an ACR instance: `az acr create --name <registry-name> --resource-group <rg> --sku Standard`
 72      * **Migrate container images:**
 73         * Import images from GCR: `az acr import --name <acr-name> --source gcr.io/<project>/<image>:<tag> --image <image>:<tag>`
 74         * Or use docker pull/push: `docker pull gcr.io/<project>/<image>` then `docker push <acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
 75      * **Update image references:**
 76         * Replace `gcr.io/<project>/<image>` with `<acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
 77         * Replace `<location>-docker.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo>/<image>` with `<acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
 78         * Update all Dockerfiles, docker-compose files, Kubernetes manifests, and Helm charts
 79      * **Configure authentication:**
 80         * **For AKS (recommended):** Enable managed identity integration: `az aks update --name <aks-cluster> --attach-acr <acr-name>`
 81         * **For other services:** Use Azure managed identities or service principals
 82         * **For local development:** Use `az acr login --name <acr-name>`
 83      * **Remove GCR-specific tooling:**
 84         * Replace gcloud docker authentication with Azure CLI or service principals
 85      * **For language packages (if using Artifact Registry for npm/Maven/Python):**
 86         * Use Azure Artifacts for package management instead of Google Artifact Registry
 87    ruleID: google-gcr-to-azure-acr-01000
 88    when:

 30            c: http://camel.apache.org/schema/spring

122    message: |-
123      To migrate a Java application that uses a Sybase database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:
124  
125      * **Choose your Azure target**:
126        * **Azure SQL Database**: The recommended target for Sybase migration, offering a fully managed PaaS service with high compatibility for most Sybase features.
127        * **Azure SQL Managed Instance**: Provides near 100% compatibility with SQL Server and better support for complex Sybase features like stored procedures and triggers.
128        * **SQL Server on Azure VMs**: For maximum compatibility when PaaS migration is not feasible due to specific Sybase dependencies.
129  
130      * **Assess migration complexity**:
131        * Use **SQL Server Migration Assistant (SSMA) for Sybase** to assess database schema compatibility and generate migration reports.
132        * Identify Sybase-specific features that need conversion (e.g., stored procedures, triggers, data types).
133        * Review T-SQL syntax differences and plan for code modifications.
134  
135      * **Migrate** the existing Sybase database:
136        * Use **SSMA for Sybase** to convert database schema and migrate data to Azure SQL Database or SQL Managed Instance.
137        * Utilize **Azure Database Migration Service (DMS)** for online migrations with minimal downtime.
138        * Test migrated database thoroughly, especially stored procedures and complex queries.
139  
140      * Update the application's **database connection** details: Modify the Java application's configuration to point to the newly provisioned Azure SQL service. Update the connection string (JDBC URL), driver class (from Sybase jConnect to SQL Server JDBC driver), hostname, port, username, and password information accordingly.
141  
142      * **Address compatibility issues**:
143        * Replace Sybase-specific SQL syntax with T-SQL equivalents.
144        * Update data type mappings (e.g., Sybase datetime to SQL Server datetime2).
145        * Modify stored procedures and functions to use T-SQL syntax.
146        * Test and update any Sybase-specific driver configurations.
147  
148      * Enable **monitoring and diagnostics**: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying Azure SQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.
149  
150      * Implement **security** measures: Apply security best practices including Azure AD authentication, transparent data encryption, and leverage Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.
151  
152      * **Backup** your data: Azure SQL Database and SQL Managed Instance provide automated backups by default. Configure retention periods and consider geo-redundant backups for enhanced data durability.
153    ruleID: openliberty-database-00003

 19    message: |-
 20      This is a JDBC URL, which describes the basic information about
 21       where and how to connect to the database.
 22       This particular URL points to a PostgreSQL database.
 23  
 24       In EAP 6, the databases are configured in these steps:
 25  
 26       1. Add the JDBC driver as an EAP 6 module. Download it [here](https://jdbc.postgresql.org/download.html).
 27       2. Create a datasource (actual values need to be changed):
 28       ```
 29       $ EAP_HOME/bin/jboss-cli --connect
 30       [standalone@localhost:9999 /] data-source add --name=ExampleDS --jndi-name=java:/ExampleDS \\
 31       --connection-url=... --driver-name=postgresql \\
 32       --user-name=... --password=...
 33       ```
 34       3. Use the datasource according to JPA 2.0 standards.

 45          namespaces: {}

 50       ```java
 51       ClientRequest request = new ClientRequest(generateURL("/linkheader/str"));
 52       request.addLink("previous chapter", "previous", "http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2", null);
 53       ClientResponse response = request.post();
 54       LinkHeader header = response.getLinkHeader();
 55       ```
 56  
 57       The following is an example of how to accomplish the same task with the RESTEasy client in RESTEasy 3.
 58  
 59       ```java
 60       ResteasyClient client = new ResteasyClientBuilder().build();
 61       Response response = client.target(generateURL("/linkheader/str")).request()
 62       .header("Link", "<http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2>; rel="previous";
 63       title="previous chapter">").post(Entity.text(new String()));
 64       javax.ws.rs.core.Link link = response.getLink("previous");
 65       ```

 77    message: |-
 78      The WebLogic `<delay-updates-until-end-of-tx>` configuration element, which defaults to `true`, is used for performance reasons to delay updates to the persistent store of all beans until the end of the transaction. When set to `false`, updates are sent to the database after each method invocation, but are not committed until the end of the transaction.  987    links: []
 988    message: |-
 989      Previous versions of Hibernate have mapped `byte[]` and `Byte[]` to Oracle’s `LONG RAW` data type (via the JDBC `LONGVARBINARY` type). Oracle have deprecated the `LONG RAW` data type for many releases - possibly as far back as 8i.
 990  
 991       Therefore it was decided to start having Hibernate map `byte[]` and `Byte[]` to `BLOB` for Oracle.
 992  
 993       However, in the interest of backwards compatibility and not breaking existing applications it was also decided to limit this change to just the `Oracle12cDialect`. So starting in 5.1 applications using `Oracle12cDialect` and implicitly mapping `byte[]` and `Byte[]` values will start seeing those handled as `BLOB` data rather than `LONG RAW` data.
 994       For existing applications that want to continue to use `Oracle12cDialect` and still continue to implicitly map `byte[]` and `Byte[]` attributes to `LONG RAW`, there is a new configuration setting you can use to enable that: `hibernate.dialect.oracle.prefer_longvarbinary`, which is `false `by default (map to `BLOB`).

 14    message: |-
 15      Sonic ESB services inherit from XQService. In Camel, this can be achieved through the simple Java Bean Camel Component.
 16  
 17       * [Camel Java Bean Component](http://camel.apache.org/bean.html)
 18    ruleID: sonic-esb-01000

 29    effort: 4
 30    labels:
 31    - source=sonic
 32    - target=fuse6+
 33    - target=fuse
 34    - sonic-esb
 35    - camel
 36    links: []
 37    message: |-
 38      Sonic ESB services leverage the service(XQServiceContext context) method to implement business logic. When messages are routed to the service, the service(XQServiceContext context) method is executed.
 39       In Camel, this is achieved by routing messages to the Java Bean via the Camel Route's Bean Component syntax.
 40  
 41       * [Camel Java Bean Component](http://camel.apache.org/bean.html)
 42       * [Camel Binding Annotations](http://camel.apache.org/parameter-binding-annotations.html)
 43  
 44       Camel's Java Bean Component can leverage annotations annotations on the method to specify how Camel Message body values are mapped to the method parameters. Additionally, the @Handler annotation can be leveraged to setup the default Java Bean method.
 45  
 46       **For example:**
 47  
 48       ```java
 49       public void service(XQServiceContext ctx) throws XQServiceException \{{
 50       ...
 51       }}
 52       ```
 53  
 54       **Should become:**
 55  
 56       ```java
 57       @Handler
 58       public void service(@Header messageHeader, @Body messageBody, Exchange exchange) \{{
 59       ...
 60       }}
 61       ```
 62  
 63       * org.apache.camel.Body
 64       * org.apache.camel.Header
 65       * org.apache.camel.Exchange

653    message: |-
654      JBoss ESB uses notifiers to transform ESB aware messages to a format that ESB-unaware services can handle. Fuse Service Works uses bi-directional gateways to transfer messages
655       via its service bindings.
656  
657       A JBoss ESB Notifier should be converted to a Fuse Service Works Service Binding.
658  
659       For example:
660  
661       ```xml
662       <service category="routerToFile" name="FileRouterListener" description="Static route file destination">
663       <actions mep="OneWay">
664       <action name="notificationAction" class="org.jboss.soa.esb.actions.Notifier">
665       <property name="okMethod" value="notifyOK"/>
666       <property name="notification-details">
667       <NotificationList type="ok">
668       <target class="NotifyFiles">
669       <file append="false" URI="/tmp/HelloWorldFileNotifierTest.log"/>
670       </target>
671       </NotificationList>
672       </property>
673       </action>
674       </actions>
675       </service>
676       ```
677  
678  
679       Could be translated to:
680  
681       ```xml
682       <sca:reference name="HelloWorld" multiplicity="0..1" promote="MyComponent/HelloWorld">
683       <camel:binding.file>
684       <camel:directory>/tmp</camel:directory>
685       <camel:fileName>HelloWorldFileNotifierTest.log</camel:fileName>
686       </camel:binding.file>
687       </sca:reference>
688       <sca:component name="MyComponent">
689       <sca:reference name="HelloWorld">
690       <sca:interface.wsdl interface="HelloWorld.wsdl#wsdl.porttype(HelloWorld)"/>
691       </sca:reference>
692       </sca:component>
693       ```

695    when:

Entity Enterprise JavaBeans 157 (EJB) \n

This rule flags entity elements in ejb-jar.xml 158 files.

\n

Entity beans are optional in the EJB 3.2 specification and 159 are not supported on Liberty or Liberty Core. The entity bean API is deprecated 160 in WebSphere Application Server traditional V8.5.5 and V9.0 and might be removed 161 in a later version.

\n

The EJBDeploy tool used to deploy applications 162 with entity beans has also been deprecated and may be removed in the future, either 163 at the same time entity beans are removed or prior.

\n

The Java Persistence 164 API (JPA) is an alternative to using EJB entity beans for new database and other 165 persistence-related operations.

\n

Upgrading entity beans can be difficult, 166 but it can be simplified if your application uses design patterns such as DTO, 167 Session Facade, and DAO.

\n
" 168 ruleID: DetectEJBEntityBeansXML 169 when: 170 builtin.xml: 171 filepaths: 172 - ejb-jar.xml 173 namespaces: {} 174 xpath: //*[local-name()='entity'] 175 - category: mandatory 176 customVariables: [] 177 description: Transaction propagation is not supported for Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB) 178 remote interfaces 179 effort: 1 180 labels: 181 - source=websphere 182 - target=openliberty 183 links: 184 - title: Open Liberty migration rules in Windup 185 url: https://www.ibm.com/docs/wamt?topic=rules-open-liberty-migration-in-windup 186 message: "
\n

Liberty does not support outbound or inbound 187 transaction propagation for EJB remote interfaces. By default, EJB beans are container-managed 188 and use the Required transaction attribute. As a result, existing 189 EJB definitions that do not specify any container-transaction properties 190 are configured by default to use transactions although they are not supported. 191

\n

This rule flags Java code that references the following EJB annotations 192 that indicate the use of remote business or home interfaces:

\n
    \n
  • javax.ejb.Remote
    • 193 \n
  • javax.ejb.RemoteHome
    • \n
\n

This rule also flags 194 the following references in the ejb-jar.xml file:

195 \n
    \n
  • <remote/>
    • \n
  • <business-remote/>
    • 196 \n
\n

The EJB specification requires products that support outbound 197 transaction propagation to still send a null transaction context. This context 198 must be rejected by EJB components that use the Required (default), 199 Mandatory , or Supports transaction attributes. A client 200 with an active global transaction cannot start an EJB bean with default transaction 201 attributes if either the client or server is on Liberty.

\n

To enable 202 the client to start the EJB bean, change the EJB bean to use either the RequiresNew 203 or NotSupported transaction attribute. Although these attributes 204 will allow the EJB bean to start, the transactional work that is done by the EJB 205 bean is not committed as part of the client transactions.

\n

Note that 206 transaction propagation is supported for EJB remote interfaces that are running 207 in the same JVM, however this may only be determined with further investigation 208 of the application behavior.

\n

Make sure remote EJB interfaces are needed

209 \n

Often EJB 2.x beans configure the remote interfaces in ejb-jar.xml even 210 when they are not used. You only need remote interfaces if you have code running 211 across two different JVMs. In WebSphere terms, this is either between two different 212 application servers or between a client application and an application server 213 running in different JVMs. CORBA information, such as an iiop:// 214 provider URL, in an EJB lookup is also an indicator that remote EJB beans are 215 being used.

\n

If you are referencing EJB beans using a remote interface 216 that are running in the same JVM, the Local interface can be used and will perform 217 better. Where possible, change annotations from @Remote to @Local and from @RemoteHome 218 to @LocalHome and test all your code scenarios. Likewise for ejb-jar.xml configuration, 219 remove the <remote/> and <business-remote/> 220 definitions and test all scenarios. While transaction propagation is supported 221 for this scenario, the best practice is to convert to using local interfaces to 222 improve performance and remove the perception that methods can be called externally 223 from the same JVM.

\n

If you really need remote interfaces

\n
Wrap 224 the EJB beans in a web service (JAX-WS)
\n

For those EJB beans that require 225 remote access, best practice is to wrap them in a web service. Refer to Annotating an EJB bean to create a web service for instructions 228 on using WebSphere Application Server Developer Tools for Eclipse to make these 229 code changes. After wrapping the EJB beans in web services, use the web service 230 client to call the EJB web service. After testing, you can remove the EJB remote 231 annotations or configuration.

\n
Handling Transaction Propagation
232 Liberty provides Web Services Atomic Transaction (WS-AT) support which enables 233 distributed global transactions. When your EJB are deployed as web services, WS-AT 234 can be used to manage the transactions. See Web Services Atomic Transaction overview for more information. 237 \n

For more information on related topics, see

\n
    \n

1  - category: optional
  2    customVariables: []
  3    description: Move persistence config to a properties file
  4    effort: 1
  5    labels:
  6    - source=java-ee
  7    - source=jakarta-ee
  8    - target=quarkus
  9    links:
 10    - title: Using Hibernate ORM and Jakarta persistence
 11      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#persistence-xml
 12    message: "It is recommended to move persistence related configuration from an XML
 13      file to a properties one.\n This allows centralization of the configuration in
 14      Quarkus. Check the link for more information.\n \n \n Datasource and persistence
 15      configurations in XML can be substituted with a single centralized properties
 16      file. Here is an example of a translation:\n \n The following datasource configuration:\n
 17      ```\n <datasources xmlns=\"http://www.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema\"\n xmlns:xsi=\"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance\"\n
 18      xsi:schemaLocation=\"http://www.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema http://docs.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema/datasources_1_0.xsd\">\n
 19      <!-- The datasource is bound into JNDI at this location. We reference\n this in
 20      META-INF/persistence.xml -->\n <datasource jndi-name=\"java:jboss/datasources/TasksJsfQuickstartDS\"\n
 21      pool-name=\"tasks-jsf-quickstart\" enabled=\"true\"\n use-java-context=\"true\">\n
 22      <connection-url>jdbc:h2:mem:tasks-jsf-quickstart;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1</connection-url>\n
 23      <driver>h2</driver>\n <security>\n <user-name>sa</user-name>\n <password>sa</password>\n
 24      </security>\n </datasource>\n </datasources>\n ```\n along with the following
 25      persistence configuration:\n ```\n <persistence version=\"2.1\"\n xmlns=\"http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence\"
 26      xmlns:xsi=\"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance\"\n xsi:schemaLocation=\"\n
 27      http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence\n http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence/persistence_2_1.xsd\">\n
 28      <persistence-unit name=\"primary\">\n <!-- We use a different datasource for tests,

425    description: Use SHA-256 in Remember Me
426    message: |
427      The `TokenBasedRememberMeServices` implementation now supports SHA-256 for the Remember Me token and this is the
428      default in Spring Security 6. This change makes the implementation more secure by default since MD5 is already proven
429      to be a weak hashing algorithm and vulnerable against collision attacks and modular differential attacks.
430    
431      The new generated tokens now have the information of which algorithm was used to generate the token and that information
432      is used in order to match it. If the algorithm name is not present, then the matchingAlgorithm property is used to check
433      the token. This allows for a smooth transition from MD5 to SHA-256.
434      
435      To opt into the new Spring Security 6 default to encode the tokens while still being able to decode tokens encoded with MD5,
436      you can set the encodingAlgorithm property to SHA-256 and the matchingAlgorithm property to MD5. See the reference
437      documentation and the API docs for more information.

500    description: Change the order value in @EnableTransactionManagement
501    message: |
502      `@EnableTransactionManagement` and `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity` have the same order value, `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. This means
503      that their order in the Spring AOP Advisor chain relative to each other is undefined.
504    
505      This is often fine since most method security expressions don’t require an open transaction to function correctly;
506      however, historically it was sometimes necessary to ensure one happens before the other by setting their order values.
507      
508      @EnableMethodSecurity does not have an order value since it publishes multiple interceptors. Indeed, it cannot
509      attempt backward-compatibility with @EnableTransactionManagement since it cannot set all the interceptors to be in the same advisor chain location.
510      
511      Instead, the values for the `@EnableMethodSecurity` interceptors are based off of an offset of 0. The `@PreFilter` interceptor
512      has an order of 100; `@PostAuthorize`, 200; and so on.
513  
514      So, if after updating you find that your method security expressions are not working due to not having an open
515      transaction, please change your transaction annotation definition from the following:

542    message: |
543      As a performance optimization, a new method was introduced to `MethodSecurityExpressionHandler` that takes a `Supplier<Authentication>` instead of an `Authentication`.
544      This allows Spring Security to defer the lookup of the `Authentication`, and is taken advantage of automatically when you use `@EnableMethodSecurity` instead of `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`.
545      
546      However, let’s say that your code extends DefaultMethodSecurityExpressionHandler and overrides
547      `createSecurityExpressionRoot(Authentication, MethodInvocation)` to return a custom `SecurityExpressionRoot` instance.
548      This will no longer work because the arrangement that `@EnableMethodSecurity` sets up calls `createEvaluationContext(Supplier<Authentication>, MethodInvocation)` instead.
549      
550      Happily, such a level of customization is often unnecessary. Instead, you can create a custom bean with the authorization methods that you need.
551  
552      For example, let’s say you are wanting a custom evaluation of `@PostAuthorize("hasAuthority('ADMIN')")`. You can create a custom `@Bean` like this one:
553      ```
554      class MyAuthorizer {
555        boolean isAdmin(MethodSecurityExpressionOperations root) {
556          boolean decision = root.hasAuthority("ADMIN");
557          // custom work ...
558          return decision;
559        }
560      }
561      ```
562      and then refer to it in the annotation like so:
563      ```

  9    when:
 10      java.dependency:

 12        upperbound: 5.5.13.Final
 13    description: Spring 6 must use at least Hibernate 5.6.x
 14    message: |
 15      Due to the Jakarta EE migration, Spring 6 must use at least Hibernate 5.6.x. To make Hibernate 5.6.x compatible with
 16      Jakarta, make sure to also switch your hibernate dependency to the `hibernate-core-jakarta` artifact:
 17      ```
 18      <dependency>
 19          <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
 20          <artifactId>hibernate-core-jakarta</artifactId>
 21          <version>5.6.15.Final</version>
 22      </dependency>
 23      ```
 24      Alternatively, consider migrating to Hibernate ORM 6.1 right away (exclusively based on `jakarta.persistence`,
 25      compatible with EE 9 as well as EE 10) which is the Hibernate version that Spring Boot 3.0 comes with.
 26      
 27      Please check the Hibernate 5.6 migration guide in the links provided.
 28    links:
 29    - title: 'Hibernate 5.5 to 5.6 migration guide'
 30      url: https://github.com/hibernate/hibernate-orm/blob/5.6/migration-guide.adoc
 31    - title: 'Spring 6.0 migration guide'

 65    category: potential
 66    effort: 5
 67    labels:
 68    - source=spring5
 69    - target=spring6+
 70    - target=hibernate6+
 71    when:
 72      and:
 73        - or:  # Check for Hibernate annotations or clob fields
 74          - java.referenced:
 75              location: ANNOTATION
 76              pattern: javax.persistence.Lob
 77          - java.referenced:
 78              location: FIELD
 79              pattern: java.sql.Clob
 80        - or:
 81          - builtin.filecontent:
 82              filePattern: .*\.(java|properties|xml)
 83              pattern: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQL81Dialect
 84          - java.dependency:
 85              lowerbound: 0.0.0
 86              name: org.postgresql.postgresql
 87    description: Changes to the DDL type for CLOB
 88    message: |
 89      Using `@Lob` or `java.sql.Clob` with PostgreSQL 8.1 dialect might require DDL type changes for CLOBs.
 90  
 91      Consider reviewing DDL generation for CLOB columns and potential migration to 'oid' type if necessary.
 92  
 93      All PostgreSQL JDBC drivers unfortunately just store the oid it created for a `java.sql.Clob` into the text column. 
 94      Although reading back the value with the CLOB API works, PostgreSQL has no knowledge of the reference to the LOB, 
 95      because the oid is not known to PostgreSQL, leading to data loss when vacuumlo (the utility to clean up unused LOBs) runs. 
 96      To avoid the data loss, it is required to use the oid type so that vacuumlo can see the reference.
 97  
 98      Updating to 5.6.2 does not require any schema or application changes by default, but we highly recommend that you migrate 
 99      existing text columns for LOBs to oid to prevent data loss due to the activity of vacuumlo. 
100    links:
101    - title: 'Hibernate 5.6 migration guide - Changes to the DDL type for CLOB'
102      url: https://github.com/hibernate/hibernate-orm/blob/5.6/migration-guide.adoc#changes-to-the-ddl-type-for-clob-in-postgresql81dialect-and-its-subclasses

 15      url: https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_jboss_enterprise_application_platform/7.0/html-single/migration_guide/#migrate_default_remote_url_connector_and_port_changes
 16    message: |-
 17      Default Remote JNDI Provider URL has changed in EAP 7. External applications using JNDI to lookup remote resources, for instance an EJB or a JMS Queue,
 18       may need to change the value for the JNDI InitialContext environment's property named `java.naming.provider.url`.
 19       The default URL scheme is now **http-remoting** instead of **remote**, and the default URL port is now **8080** instead of **4447**.
 20  
 21       As an example, consider the application server host is localhost, then clients previously accessing EAP 6 would use
 22  
 23       ```
 24       java.naming.factory.initial=org.jboss.naming.remote.client.InitialContextFactory
 25       java.naming.provider.url=remote://localhost:4447
 26       ```
 27  
 28       while clients now accessing EAP 7 should use instead
 29  
 30       ```
 31       java.naming.factory.initial=org.jboss.naming.remote.client.InitialContextFactory
 32       java.naming.provider.url=http-remoting://localhost:8080
 33       ```
 34    ruleID: eap6-08000

 36      builtin.filecontent:
 37        filePattern: .*\.(java|properties|xml)
 38        pattern: remote://.*:\d*

689  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-security-00140
690    category: mandatory
691    effort: 3
692    labels:
693      - source=spring5
694      - source=spring-boot2
695      - target=spring6+
696      - target=spring-boot3+
697    when:
698      java.referenced:
699        pattern: org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity.authorizeRequests
700        location: METHOD_CALL
701    description: Ensure that all requests have defined authorization rules
702    message: |
703      In Spring Security 5.8 and earlier, requests with no authorization rule are permitted by default. It is a stronger
704      security position to deny by default, thus requiring that authorization rules be clearly defined for every endpoint.
705      As such, in 6.0, Spring Security by default denies any request that is missing an authorization rule.
706      
707      The simplest way to prepare for this change is to introduce an appropriate `anyRequest` rule as the last authorization rule.
708      The recommendation is `denyAll` since that is the implied 6.0 default.
709      
710      Adding `denyAll` to the end looks like changing:
711      ```
712      http
713      .authorizeRequests((authorize) -> authorize
714          .filterSecurityInterceptorOncePerRequest(true)
715          .mvcMatchers("/app/**").hasRole("APP")
716          // ...
717      )
718      // ...
719      ```
720      to:
721      ```
722      http
723      .authorizeRequests((authorize) -> authorize
724          .filterSecurityInterceptorOncePerRequest(true)
725          .mvcMatchers("/app/**").hasRole("APP")
726          // ...
727          .anyRequest().denyAll()
728      )
729      // ...
730      ```
731  
732    links:
733      - title: 'Ensure that all requests have defined authorization rules'
734        url: https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/5.8/migration/servlet/authorization.html#_ensure_that_all_requests_have_defined_authorization_rules

737  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-security-00150
738    category: mandatory
739    effort: 3
740    labels:
741      - source=spring5
742      - source=spring-boot2
743      - target=spring6+
744      - target=spring-boot3+
745    when:
746      builtin.filecontent:
747        filePattern: .*\.java
748        pattern: \".*hasIpAddress\(.*\"
749    description: Migrate hasIpAddress to access(AuthorizationManager)
750    message: |
751      `hasIpAddress` has no DSL equivalent in `authorizeHttpRequests`. As such, you need to change any calls to `hasIpAddress` to using an `AuthorizationManager`.
752      
753      First, construct an IpAddressMatcher like so:
754      ```
755      IpAddressMatcher hasIpAddress = new IpAddressMatcher("127.0.0.1");
756      ```
757      and then change from this:
758      ```
759      http
760      .authorizeRequests((authorize) -> authorize
761          .mvcMatchers("/app/**").access("hasIpAddress('127.0.0.1')")
762          .anyRequest().denyAll()
763      )
764      // ...
765      ```
766      to this:
767      ```
768      http
769      .authorizeHttpRequests((authorize) -> authorize
770          .requestMatchers("/app/**").access((authentication, context) ->
771              new AuthorizationDecision(hasIpAddress.matches(context.getRequest()))
772          // ...
773          .anyRequest().denyAll()
774      )
775      // ...
776      ```
777

780        url: https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/5.8/migration/servlet/authorization.html#_migrate_hasipaddress_to_accessauthorizationmanager

784  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-security-00160
785    category: optional
786    effort: 3
787    labels:
788      - source=spring5
789      - source=spring-boot2
790      - target=spring6+
791      - target=spring-boot3+
792    when:
793      java.referenced:
794  #      pattern: ExpressionInterceptUrlRegistry.access
795  #      pattern: ExpressionUrlAuthorizationConfigurer.ExpressionInterceptUrlRegistry.access(String)
796  #      TODO: weak rule. The patterns above does not seem to work, so had to simplify it.
797        pattern: access(String)
798        location: METHOD_CALL
799    description: Migrate SpEL expressions to AuthorizationManager
800    message: |
801      For authorization rules, Java tends to be easier to test and maintain than SpEL. As such, authorizeHttpRequests
802      does not have a method for declaring a String SpEL. Instead, you can implement your own AuthorizationManager
803      implementation or use WebExpressionAuthorizationManager.
804  
805      If you have the following SpEL:
806      ```
807      http
808      .authorizeRequests((authorize) -> authorize
809          .filterSecurityInterceptorOncePerRequest(true)
810          .mvcMatchers("/complicated/**").access("hasRole('ADMIN') || hasAuthority('SCOPE_read')")
811          // ...
812          .anyRequest().denyAll()
813      )
814      // ...
815      ```
816      you can compose your own AuthorizationManager with Spring Security authorization primitives like so:
817      ```
818      http
819      .authorizeHttpRequests((authorize) -> authorize
820          .shouldFilterAllDispatcherTypes(false)
821          .mvcMatchers("/complicated/**").access(anyOf(hasRole("ADMIN"), hasAuthority("SCOPE_read"))
822          // ...
823          .anyRequest().denyAll()
824      )
825      // ...
826      ```
827

830        url: https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/5.8/migration/servlet/authorization.html#_migrate_spel_expressions_to_authorizationmanager

 39

 41

Using Azure Blob Storage provides a scalable object store for data objects, such as text or binary files, accessible directly in your code.
 43

 45  
 46       * **Caching**: Use Azure Cache for Redis as a cache backing service.
 47

 90       To migrate a Java application that uses file system to Azure:
 91  
 92       * **Identify the usage of the file system**: Find any instances where your services write to and/or read from the local file system. Identify where short-term/temporary files are written and read, which require ephemeral storage, and where long-lived files are written and read, which require persistent storage. Ephemeral storage only persists until the cloud environment is restarted, while persistent storage is required for data that needs to persist across restarts.
 93  
 94       The following recommendations depend on the function of the file in local storage:
 95  
 96       * **Reading/writing files**: If persistent storage is needed, consider using Azure File Share or Azure Blob Storage. Mounting an Azure File Share allows your application to access files via the mount location. Using Azure Blob Storage provides a scalable object store for data objects, such as text or binary files, accessible directly in your code.
 97  
 98       * **Logging**: Log to standard output and use Azure Monitor to collect and analyze the logs.
 99  
100       * **Caching**: Use Azure Cache for Redis as a cache backing service.
101  
102       * **Configuration**: Store configuration in Azure App Configuration instead of using the file system. Also store configuration settings in environment variables so that they can be updated without code changes.
103    ruleID: azure-file-system-03000
104    when:
105      builtin.filecontent:

107        pattern: ^\/home\/[\w0-9_\/-]*

 24      Scheduler tasks or Unix cron jobs can't be used with cloud service like Azure
 25      App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service.\n These Azure services
 26      won't prevent you from deploying an application containing scheduled tasks internally.\n
 27      However, if your application is scaled out, the same scheduled job may run more
 28      than once per scheduled period.\n This situation can lead to unintended consequences.\n
 29      \n To migrate a Java application that uses scheduled jobs to Azure, you can follow
 30      these recommendations:\n\n * **Identify scheduled jobs**: Inventory any scheduled
 31      tasks running on the production server(s), inside or outside your application
 32      code. Search the application code for references to Quartz, @Scheduled annotation,
 33      or cron expressions.\n \n * **Remove scheduled jobs**: Remove the scheduled jobs.
 34      If you need to run scheduled jobs, you can use Azure Container Apps jobs. Azure
 35      Container Apps jobs allow you to run containerized tasks that execute for a finite
 36      duration and exit. You can trigger a job manually, schedule their execution, or
 37      trigger their execution based on events."

 27    message: |-
 28      To migrate a Java application that uses a MySQL database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:
 29  
 30       * Use a managed **Azure Database for MySQL**: For that create a managed MySQL database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements for performance, storage, and availability.
 31  
 32       * **Migrate** the existing MySQL database: For that you can use the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) to perform an online migration with minimal downtime.
 33  
 34       * Update the application's **database connection** details: Modify the Java application's configuration to point to the newly provisioned Azure Database for MySQL. Update the connection string, hostname, port, username, and password information accordingly.
 35  
 36       * Enable **monitoring and diagnostics**: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying MySQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.
 37  
 38       * Implement **security** measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the MySQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.
 39  
 40       * **Backup** your data: Azure Database for MySQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

 54    links:
 55    - title: Azure Container Registry documentation
 56      url: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/
 57    - title: Migrate from Google Container Registry to Azure Container Registry
 58      url: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-import-images
 59    - title: Azure Container Registry best practices
 60      url: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-registry/container-registry-best-practices
 61    message: |-
 62      The application uses Google Container Registry (gcr.io) or Google Artifact Registry ([location]-docker.pkg.dev) for container images.
 63  
 64      **Common patterns detected may include:**
 65      * Container image references in Dockerfiles and docker-compose files
 66      * Kubernetes manifests (Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs, Pods) with GCR images
 67      * Configuration files referencing GCR endpoints
 68  
 69      **To migrate to Azure Container Registry (ACR):**
 70      * **Provision Azure Container Registry:**
 71         * Create an ACR instance: `az acr create --name <registry-name> --resource-group <rg> --sku Standard`
 72      * **Migrate container images:**
 73         * Import images from GCR: `az acr import --name <acr-name> --source gcr.io/<project>/<image>:<tag> --image <image>:<tag>`
 74         * Or use docker pull/push: `docker pull gcr.io/<project>/<image>` then `docker push <acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
 75      * **Update image references:**
 76         * Replace `gcr.io/<project>/<image>` with `<acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
 77         * Replace `<location>-docker.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo>/<image>` with `<acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
 78         * Update all Dockerfiles, docker-compose files, Kubernetes manifests, and Helm charts
 79      * **Configure authentication:**
 80         * **For AKS (recommended):** Enable managed identity integration: `az aks update --name <aks-cluster> --attach-acr <acr-name>`
 81         * **For other services:** Use Azure managed identities or service principals
 82         * **For local development:** Use `az acr login --name <acr-name>`
 83      * **Remove GCR-specific tooling:**
 84         * Replace gcloud docker authentication with Azure CLI or service principals
 85      * **For language packages (if using Artifact Registry for npm/Maven/Python):**
 86         * Use Azure Artifacts for package management instead of Google Artifact Registry
 87    ruleID: google-gcr-to-azure-acr-01000
 88    when:
 89      or:
 90      - builtin.filecontent:
 91          filePattern: (?i)(dockerfile|\.dockerignore|docker-compose\.ya?ml|.*\.ya?ml|.*\.json|\.properties|pom\.xml|build\.gradle|package\.json|requirements\.txt|\.npmrc|\.pypirc|Makefile|.*\.sh|.*\.ps1)$
 92          pattern: (gcr\.io|[a-z]+-docker\.pkg\.dev)
