 51    links:
 52    - title: Remote JNDI URL in EAP 7
 53      url: https://access.redhat.com/documentation/en-us/red_hat_jboss_enterprise_application_platform/7.0/html-single/migration_guide/#update_the_default_remote_connection_port
 54    message: |-
 55      The default remote connection port has changed in **jboss-ejb-client.properties** from '4447' to '8080'.
 56  
 57       In EAP 6, the jboss-ejb-client.properties file looked similar to the following:
 58  
 59       ```
 60       remote.connectionprovider.create.options.org.xnio.Options.SSL_ENABLED=false
 61       remote.connections=default
 62       remote.connection.default.host=localhost
 63       remote.connection.default.port=4447
 64       remote.connection.default.connect.options.org.xnio.Options.SASL_POLICY_NOANONYMOUS=false
 65       ```
 66  
 67       In EAP 7, the properties file looks like this:
 68  
 69       ```
 70       remote.connectionprovider.create.options.org.xnio.Options.SSL_ENABLED=false
 71       remote.connections=default
 72       remote.connection.default.host=localhost
 73       remote.connection.default.port=8080
 74       remote.connection.default.connect.options.org.xnio.Options.SASL_POLICY_NOANONYMOUS=false
 75       ```
 76    ruleID: eap6-08001
 77    when:
 78      builtin.filecontent:
 79        filePattern: jboss-ejb-client\.properties
 80        pattern: remote.connection..*.port(.*(?!8080)\d{4})

 96    message: |-
 97      The default remote connection port has changed from '4447' to '8080'.
 98  
 99       In EAP 6, Remote EJB client Java code looks like the following:
100  
101       ```java

103       properties.put("remote.connection.default.port", "4447");

105

 45    message: |-
 46      Replace class `org.jboss.resteasy.client.ClientRequest` with `org.jboss.resteasy.client.jaxrs.ResteasyClient`.
 47  
 48       The following is an example of how to send a link header with the RESTEasy client in EAP 6 with RESTEasy 2.3.x.
 49  
 50       ```java
 51       ClientRequest request = new ClientRequest(generateURL("/linkheader/str"));
 52       request.addLink("previous chapter", "previous", "http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2", null);
 53       ClientResponse response = request.post();
 54       LinkHeader header = response.getLinkHeader();
 55       ```
 56  
 57       The following is an example of how to accomplish the same task with the RESTEasy client in RESTEasy 3.
 58  
 59       ```java
 60       ResteasyClient client = new ResteasyClientBuilder().build();
 61       Response response = client.target(generateURL("/linkheader/str")).request()
 62       .header("Link", "<http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2>; rel="previous";
 63       title="previous chapter">").post(Entity.text(new String()));
 64       javax.ws.rs.core.Link link = response.getLink("previous");
 65       ```

 75        to the JBoss Enterprise Application Platform Equivalent
 76      url: https://access.redhat.com/articles/1326823
 77    message: |-
 78      The WebLogic `<delay-updates-until-end-of-tx>` configuration element, which defaults to `true`, is used for performance reasons to delay updates to the persistent store of all beans until the end of the transaction. When set to `false`, updates are sent to the database after each method invocation, but are not committed until the end of the transaction. This allows other processes to access the persisted data while the transaction is waiting to be completed.
 79  
 80       In JBoss EAP 6+, you can achieve the same behavior by specifying the `<sync-on-commit-only>` in the jbosscmp-jdbc.xml file.

 19    message: "The way in which Hibernate determines implicit names for sequences and
 20      tables associated with identifier generation has changed in 6.0 which may affect
 21      migrating applications. \n As of 6.0, Hibernate by default creates a sequence
 22      per entity hierarchy instead of a single sequence hibernate_sequence. \n Due to
 23      this change, users that previously used `@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationStrategy.AUTO)`
 24      or simply `@GeneratedValue` (since `AUTO` is the default), need to ensure that
 25      the database now contains sequences for every entity, named `<entity name>_seq`.
 26      For an entity Person, a sequence person_seq is expected to exist. \n It’s best
 27      to run hbm2ddl (e.g. by temporarily setting `hbm2ddl.auto=create`) to obtain a
 28      list of DDL statements for the sequences."

 30    message: "When migrating an application that relies on the file system to Azure,
 31      it's important to consider the limitations of local storage in a cloud environment.\n
 32      An application running inside a container could lose access to a file in local
 33      storage.\n\n The following recommendations depend on the function of the file
 34      in local storage:\n * Determine the **storage needs** for your application: Ephemeral
 35      storage or persistent storage. Ephemeral storage only persists until the cloud
 36      environment is restarted. Persistent storage is required for data that needs to
 37      persist across restarts.\n \n * If persistent storage is needed, consider **mounting
 38      Azure File Share** or **using Azure Blob Storage**. Mount Azure file share allows
 39      your application to access files via the mount location. Azure blob storage is
 40      a scalable object store for data objects, such as text or binary files.\n\n *
 41      **Logging**: Log to standard output and use Azure Monitor to collect and analyze
 42      the logs.\n\n * **Caching**: Use Azure Cache for Redis as a cache backing service.\n\n
 43      * **Configuration**: Store configuration in Azure App Configuration instead of
 44      using the file system. Also store configuration settings in environment variables
 45      so that they can be updated without code changes."

 14    message: |-
 15      Sonic ESB services inherit from XQService. In Camel, this can be achieved through the simple Java Bean Camel Component.
 16

 28    description: Reference to com.sonicsw.xq.XQServiceContext
 29    effort: 4
 30    labels:
 31    - source=sonic
 32    - target=fuse6+
 33    - target=fuse
 34    - sonic-esb
 35    - camel
 36    links: []
 37    message: |-
 38      Sonic ESB services leverage the service(XQServiceContext context) method to implement business logic. When messages are routed to the service, the service(XQServiceContext context) method is executed.
 39       In Camel, this is achieved by routing messages to the Java Bean via the Camel Route's Bean Component syntax.
 40  
 41       * [Camel Java Bean Component](http://camel.apache.org/bean.html)
 42       * [Camel Binding Annotations](http://camel.apache.org/parameter-binding-annotations.html)
 43  
 44       Camel's Java Bean Component can leverage annotations annotations on the method to specify how Camel Message body values are mapped to the method parameters. Additionally, the @Handler annotation can be leveraged to setup the default Java Bean method.
 45  
 46       **For example:**
 47  
 48       ```java
 49       public void service(XQServiceContext ctx) throws XQServiceException \{{
 50       ...
 51       }}
 52       ```
 53  
 54       **Should become:**
 55  
 56       ```java
 57       @Handler
 58       public void service(@Header messageHeader, @Body messageBody, Exchange exchange) \{{
 59       ...
 60       }}
 61       ```
 62  
 63       * org.apache.camel.Body
 64       * org.apache.camel.Header
 65       * org.apache.camel.Exchange
 66    ruleID: sonic-esb-02000
 67    when:

 69      - java.referenced:
 70          location: TYPE
 71          pattern: com.sonicsw.xq.XQServiceContext
 72      - java.referenced:

 74          pattern: com.sonicsw.xq.XQServiceContext

 93  
 94       ```java

 97       //leverage injected properties
 98       }}
 99       ```

 23    - title: Java 11 AWTPermission api
 24      url: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.desktop/java/awt/AWTPermission.html
 25    message: |-
 26      Due to modularisation, the methods `java.lang.SecurityManager.checkAwtEventQueueAccess()`,
 27       `java.lang.SecurityManager.checkSystemClipboardAccess()` and
 28       `java.lang.SecurityManager.checkTopLevelWindow(java.lang.Object)`

 30

 32  
 33       `java.lang.SecurityManager.checkAwtEventQueueAccess()` --> `java.lang.SecurityManager.checkPermission(new AWTPermission("accessEventQueue"))`
 34       `java.lang.SecurityManager.checkSystemClipboardAccess()` --> `java.lang.SecurityManager.checkPermission(new AWTPermission("accessClipboard"))`
 35       `java.lang.SecurityManager.checkTopLevelWindow(java.lang.Object) --> java.lang.SecurityManager.checkPermission(new AWTPermission("showWindowWithoutWarningBanner"))`

 54    message: |-
 55      The `sun.misc.Unsafe` API is scheduled for removal in the long term, and some of its methods have been removed. In short term, please consider the following:
 56  
 57       - The `get` and `put` methods have equivalents that take long offsets (OpenJDK 8's version of the removed methods just casts the int offsets and used the long versions).
 58       - `fieldOffset(Field)` should be replaced by `staticFieldOffset(Field)` and `ObjectFieldOffset(Field)`.
 59       - `staticFieldBase(Class)` should be replaced by asking for a specific field with `staticFieldBase(Field)`. The removed method only returned the address of the first static field in the class and relied on the assumption that the JVM stored all statics together, which may not be true.
 60       - `tryMonitorEnter(Object)` and `monitorExit(Object)` can be replaced with use of the Java synchronized primitives, as illustrated in the test changes for JDK-8054494 (see links below).
 61  
 62       In the long term, please consider using Variable Handles (see the link below)

 19      url: https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/9-relnotes.html#JDK-6516909
 20    message: |-
 21      The system property `sun.lang.ClassLoader.allowArraySyntax` was introduced as a temporary workaround to give customers time to remove their source dependency on calling `ClassLoader.loadClass` with the array syntax that is not supported since JDK 6. This temporary workaround is removed in JDK 9 and setting `sun.lang.ClassLoader.allowArraySyntax` system property will have no effect to `ClassLoader.loadClass`. Existing code that calls `ClassLoader.loadClass` to create a Class object of an array class shall be replaced with `Class.forName`; otherwise it will get `ClassNotFoundException`.

 21      The following APIs have been deprecated:
 22

 20    message: |-
 21      Legacy `java.lang.ThreadGroup` has been degraded in this release. It is no longer possible to explicitly destroy a thread group. In its place, ThreadGroup is changed to no longer keep a strong reference to subgroups. A thread group is thus eligible to be GC'ed when there are no live threads in the group and nothing else is keeping the thread group alive.
 22  
 23      The behavior of several methods, deprecated for removal in prior releases, are changed as follows:
 24  
 25      * The destroy method does nothing.
 26  
 27      * The isDestroyed method returns false.
 28  
 29      * The setDaemon and isDaemon methods set/get a daemon status that is not used for anything.
 30  
 31      * The suspend, resume, and stop methods throw UnsupportedOperationException.

 20    message: |-
 21      The `ClassLoader` parameter is no longer ignored in `javax.xml.stream` factories.

1  - category: optional
  2    customVariables: []
  3    description: Move persistence config to a properties file
  4    effort: 1
  5    labels:
  6    - source=java-ee
  7    - source=jakarta-ee
  8    - target=quarkus
  9    links:
 10    - title: Using Hibernate ORM and Jakarta persistence
 11      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#persistence-xml
 12    message: "It is recommended to move persistence related configuration from an XML
 13      file to a properties one.\n This allows centralization of the configuration in
 14      Quarkus. Check the link for more information.\n \n \n Datasource and persistence
 15      configurations in XML can be substituted with a single centralized properties
 16      file. Here is an example of a translation:\n \n The following datasource configuration:\n
 17      ```\n <datasources xmlns=\"http://www.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema\"\n xmlns:xsi=\"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance\"\n
 18      xsi:schemaLocation=\"http://www.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema http://docs.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema/datasources_1_0.xsd\">\n
 19      <!-- The datasource is bound into JNDI at this location. We reference\n this in
 20      META-INF/persistence.xml -->\n <datasource jndi-name=\"java:jboss/datasources/TasksJsfQuickstartDS\"\n
 21      pool-name=\"tasks-jsf-quickstart\" enabled=\"true\"\n use-java-context=\"true\">\n
 22      <connection-url>jdbc:h2:mem:tasks-jsf-quickstart;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1</connection-url>\n
 23      <driver>h2</driver>\n <security>\n <user-name>sa</user-name>\n <password>sa</password>\n
 24      </security>\n </datasource>\n </datasources>\n ```\n along with the following
 25      persistence configuration:\n ```\n <persistence version=\"2.1\"\n xmlns=\"http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence\"
 26      xmlns:xsi=\"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance\"\n xsi:schemaLocation=\"\n
 27      http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence\n http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence/persistence_2_1.xsd\">\n
 28      <persistence-unit name=\"primary\">\n <!-- We use a different datasource for tests,
 29      so as to not overwrite\n production data. This is an unmanaged data source, backed
 30      by H2, an in memory\n database. Production applications should use a managed datasource.
 31      -->\n <!-- The datasource is deployed as WEB-INF/test-ds.xml,\n you can find it
 32      in the source at src/test/resources/test-ds.xml -->\n <jta-data-source>java:jboss/datasources/TasksJsfQuickstartDS</jta-data-source>\n
 33      <properties>\n <!-- Properties for Hibernate -->\n <property name=\"hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto\"
 34      value=\"create-drop\" />\n <property name=\"hibernate.show_sql\" value=\"false\"
 35      />\n </properties>\n </persistence-unit>\n </persistence>\n ```\n can be translated
 36      to:\n ```\n quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:tasks-jsf-quickstart;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1\n
 37      quarkus.datasource.db-kind=h2\n quarkus.datasource.username=sa\n quarkus.datasource.password=sa\n\n
 38      quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation=drop-and-create\n ```"
 39    ruleID: persistence-to-quarkus-00000
 40    when:
 41      or:
 42      - builtin.file:
 43          pattern: persistence\.xml
 44      - builtin.file:
 45          pattern: .*-ds\.xml
 46  - category: potential
 47    customVariables: []
 48    description: '@Produces cannot annotate an EntityManager'
 49    effort: 1
 50    labels:
 51    - source=java-ee
 52    - source=jakarta-ee
 53    - target=quarkus
 54    links:
 55    - title: Using Hibernate ORM and Jakarta persistence
 56      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#persistence-xml
 57    - title: Setting up and configuring Hibernate ORM
 58      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#setting-up-and-configuring-hibernate-orm
 59    message: "In JavaEE/JakartaEE, using `@PersistenceContext` was needed in order to
 60      inject a data source. Quarkus, on the other hand,\n will create the bean automatically
 61      just by correctly setting up your datasource, so the `@PersistenceContext` annotation can be removed. \nThis also makes having a `@Produces`
 62      annotation\n on the `EntityManager` illegal in Quarkus.\n \n If you are using
 63      a `@Produces` annotation for your EntityManager, and it is not needed after configuring
 64      your datasource, remove it and `@Inject` the EntityManager.\n Otherwise, if the
 65      producer is still needed, please create a qualification for your produced `EntityManager`,
 66      as well as every injection point for the EM.\n \n For instance, you can create
 67      an `ExtendedContext` qualifier:\n ```\n @Qualifier\n @Target({{ ElementType.TYPE,
 68      ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.PARAMETER }})\n @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)\n
 69      public @interface ExtendedContext {{ ... }}\n ```\n and then inject your entity
 70      managers:\n ```\n @ExtendedContext\n public EntityManager getEm() {{\n return
 71      em;\n }}\n ```"
 72    ruleID: persistence-to-quarkus-00011
 73    when:
 74      and:
 75      - java.referenced:
 76          location: IMPORT
 77          pattern: javax.enterprise.inject.Produces
 78        as: file
 79        ignore: true
 80      - java.referenced:
 81          location: IMPORT
 82          pattern: javax.persistence.EntityManager
 83        from: file

1  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-removed-apis-00001
  2    category: mandatory
  3    effort: 5
  4    labels:
  5    - source=spring5
  6    - target=spring6+
  7    - source=spring-boot2
  8    - target=spring-boot3+
  9    when:
 10      or:
 11      - java.referenced:
 12          pattern: org.springframework.cache.ehcache*
 13          location: IMPORT
 14      - java.dependency:
 15          name: net.sf.ehcache.ehcache
 16          upperbound: 2.10.9.2
 17    description: Spring Framework 6.0 has dropped support for EhCache 2.x
 18    message: |
 19      The org.springframework.cache.ehcache package has been removed as it was providing support for
 20      Ehcache 2.x - with this version, `net.sf.ehcache` is using Java EE APIs and is about to be End Of Life'd.
 21      Ehcache 3 is the direct replacement. Please revisit your dependency management to use `org.ehcache:ehcache`
 22      (with the jakarta classifier) instead and look into the official migration guide or reach out to the ehcache
 23      community for assistance.
 24      
 25      There is no renewed support or helpers for EhCache 3.0 integration anymore, and the `org.springframework.cache.ehcache`
 26      package has been removed. Instead, you can either use the JCache API (JSR-107) or EhCache 3's native API.
 27      
 28      If you want to use the JCache (JSR-107) integration, Spring's caching abstraction allows for it:
 29      
 30      1. Enable Caching in Spring as usual:
 31      ```java
 32      @Configuration
 33      @EnableCaching
 34      public class CacheConfig {
 35          // CacheManager bean configuration goes here
 36      }
 37      ```
 38      2. Configure a JCache `CacheManager`:
 39      ```java
 40      import javax.cache.Caching;
 41      import javax.cache.spi.CachingProvider;
 42      import org.springframework.cache.annotation.EnableCaching;
 43      import org.springframework.cache.jcache.JCacheCacheManager;
 44  
 45      @Configuration
 46      @EnableCaching
 47      public class CacheConfig {
 48          @Bean
 49          public JCacheCacheManager cacheManager() {
 50              CachingProvider cachingProvider = Caching.getCachingProvider();
 51              javax.cache.CacheManager ehCacheManager = cachingProvider.getCacheManager();
 52              return new JCacheCacheManager(ehCacheManager);
 53          }
 54      }
 55      ```
 56      
 57      Additionally, you may need to adapt your Ehcache 2.x XML configuration to be compatible with Ehcache 3.x
 58      if you were previously using XML-based cache configurations.
 59      
 60      For specifics on how to migrate from Ehcache 2 to 3, please check the link provided.
 61    links:
 62    - title: 'Spring 6.0 migration guide'
 63      url: https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/wiki/Spring-Framework-6.0-Release-Notes#removed-apis
 64    - title: 'Ehcache 2 to 3 migration guide'
 65      url: https://www.ehcache.org/documentation/3.10/migration-guide.html

  2    category: optional
  3    effort: 1
  4    labels:

  6      - target=spring-boot3+
  7    when:
  8      builtin.filecontent:
  9        filePattern: .*\.properties
 10        pattern: server\.max-http-header-size
 11    description: 'server.max-http-header-size has been deprecated'
 12    message: |
 13      Previously, the `server.max-http-header-size` was treated inconsistently across the four supported embedded web
 14      servers. When using Jetty, Netty, or Undertow it would configure the max HTTP request header size.
 15      When using Tomcat it would configure the max HTTP request and response header sizes.
 16  
 17      To address this inconsistency, `server.max-http-header-size` has been deprecated and a replacement,
 18      `server.max-http-request-header-size`, has been introduced. Both properties now only apply to the request header
 19      size, irrespective of the underlying web server.
 20  
 21      To limit the max header size of an HTTP response on Tomcat or Jetty (the only two servers that support such
 22      a setting), use a `WebServerFactoryCustomizer`.
 23  
 24    links:
 25      - title: 'Spring Boot 3.0 Migration Guide - Web application changes'
 26        url: https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/wiki/Spring-Boot-3.0-Migration-Guide#servermax-http-header-size

 64  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-data-access-00003
 65    category: potential
 66    effort: 5
 67    labels:
 68    - source=spring5
 69    - target=spring6+
 70    - target=hibernate6+
 71    when:
 72      and:
 73        - or:  # Check for Hibernate annotations or clob fields
 74          - java.referenced:
 75              location: ANNOTATION
 76              pattern: javax.persistence.Lob
 77          - java.referenced:
 78              location: FIELD
 79              pattern: java.sql.Clob
 80        - or:
 81          - builtin.filecontent:
 82              filePattern: .*\.(java|properties|xml)
 83              pattern: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQL81Dialect
 84          - java.dependency:
 85              lowerbound: 0.0.0
 86              name: org.postgresql.postgresql
 87    description: Changes to the DDL type for CLOB
 88    message: |
 89      Using `@Lob` or `java.sql.Clob` with PostgreSQL 8.1 dialect might require DDL type changes for CLOBs.
 90  
 91      Consider reviewing DDL generation for CLOB columns and potential migration to 'oid' type if necessary.
 92  
 93      All PostgreSQL JDBC drivers unfortunately just store the oid it created for a `java.sql.Clob` into the text column. 
 94      Although reading back the value with the CLOB API works, PostgreSQL has no knowledge of the reference to the LOB, 
 95      because the oid is not known to PostgreSQL, leading to data loss when vacuumlo (the utility to clean up unused LOBs) runs. 
 96      To avoid the data loss, it is required to use the oid type so that vacuumlo can see the reference.
 97  
 98      Updating to 5.6.2 does not require any schema or application changes by default, but we highly recommend that you migrate 
 99      existing text columns for LOBs to oid to prevent data loss due to the activity of vacuumlo. 
100    links:
101    - title: 'Hibernate 5.6 migration guide - Changes to the DDL type for CLOB'
102      url: https://github.com/hibernate/hibernate-orm/blob/5.6/migration-guide.adoc#changes-to-the-ddl-type-for-clob-in-postgresql81dialect-and-its-subclasses

 11        pattern: org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping
 12        location: ANNOTATION
 13        annotated:
 14          elements:
 15            - name: value
 16              value: '.*[^\/]$'
 17    description: Trailing slack matching has changed in Spring 6.0
 18    message: |
 19      As of Spring Framework 6.0, the trailing slash matching configuration option has been deprecated and its default
 20      value set to false. This means that previously, the following controller would match both
 21      "GET /some/greeting" and "GET /some/greeting/":
 22    
 23      ```java
 24      @RestController
 25      public class MyController {
 26          @GetMapping("/some/greeting")
 27              public String greeting() {
 28              return "Hello";
 29          }
 30      }
 31      ```
 32    
 33      As of this Spring Framework change, "GET /some/greeting/" doesn't match anymore by default and will result in an
 34      HTTP 404 error. Developers should instead configure explicit redirects/rewrites through a proxy, a Servlet/web
 35      filter, or even declare the additional route explicitly on the controller handler
 36      (like @GetMapping("/some/greeting", "/some/greeting/") for more targeted cases.
 37      Until your application fully adapts to this change, you can change the default with the following
 38      global Spring MVC configuration:
 39      
 40      ```java
 41      @Configuration
 42      public class WebConfiguration implements WebMvcConfigurer {
 43          @Override
 44          public void configurePathMatch(PathMatchConfigurer configurer) {
 45              configurer.setUseTrailingSlashMatch(true);
 46          }
 47      }
 48      ```

  2    category: mandatory

 11    when:
 12      java.referenced:
 13        pattern: org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter
 14        location: INHERITANCE
 15    description: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter has been removed in Spring Security 6.0
 16    message: |
 17      `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` has been removed in Spring Security 6.0. Now, to configure security,
 18      instead of extending `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter`, define a `SecurityFilterChain` bean in a `@Configuration`
 19      class:
 20      
 21      Before:
 22      ```java
 23      @Configuration
 24      @EnableWebSecurity
 25      public class SecurityConfig extends WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter {
 26          @Override
 27          protected void configure(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
 28              http
 29                  .authorizeRequests()
 30                      .antMatchers("/public").permitAll()
 31                      .anyRequest().authenticated()
 32                  .and()
 33                  .formLogin();
 34          }
 35      }
 36      ```
 37      
 38      After:
 39      ```java
 40      @Configuration
 41      @EnableWebSecurity
 42      public class SecurityConfig {
 43          @Bean
 44          public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
 45              http
 46              .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
 47                  .requestMatchers("/public").permitAll()
 48                  .anyRequest().authenticated()
 49              )
 50              .formLogin(withDefaults());
 51              return http.build();
 52          }
 53      }
 54      ```

 61  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-security-00010
 62    category: potential
 63    effort: 5
 64    labels:
 65      - source=spring5
 66      - source=spring-boot2
 67      - target=spring6+
 68      - target=spring-boot3+
 69    when:
 70      or:
 71      - java.referenced:
 72          pattern: org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder.getContext()
 73          location: METHOD_CALL
 74      - java.referenced:
 75          pattern: org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder.setContext(*)
 76          location: METHOD_CALL
 77    description: SecurityContext not automatically saved anymore
 78    message: |
 79      In Spring Security 5, the default behavior is for the SecurityContext to automatically be saved to the
 80      SecurityContextRepository using the SecurityContextPersistenceFilter. Saving must be done just prior to the
 81      HttpServletResponse being committed and just before SecurityContextPersistenceFilter. Unfortunately, automatic
 82      persistence of the SecurityContext can surprise users when it is done prior to the request completing (i.e. just
 83      prior to committing the HttpServletResponse). It also is complex to keep track of the state to determine if a
 84      save is necessary causing unnecessary writes to the SecurityContextRepository (i.e. HttpSession) at times.
 85    
 86      In Spring Security 6, the default behavior is that the SecurityContextHolderFilter will only read the SecurityContext
 87      from SecurityContextRepository and populate it in the SecurityContextHolder. Users now must explicitly save the
 88      SecurityContext with the SecurityContextRepository if they want the SecurityContext to persist between requests.
 89      This removes ambiguity and improves performance by only requiring writing to the SecurityContextRepository
 90      (i.e. HttpSession) when it is necessary.
 91      
 92      So for instance, the following code:
 93      ```java
 94      SecurityContextHolder.setContext(securityContext);
 95      ```
 96      
 97      should now be:
 98      ```java
 99      SecurityContextHolder.setContext(securityContext);
100      securityContextRepository.saveContext(securityContext, httpServletRequest, httpServletResponse);
101      ```
102      
103      so that the context is explicitly saved.
104  
105    links:
106      - title: 'Session Management Migrations - Spring Security'
107        url: https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/5.8/migration/servlet/session-management.html#_require_explicit_saving_of_securitycontextrepository

136    description: Change HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository to DelegatingSecurityContextRepository
137    message: |
138      In Spring Security 5, the default SecurityContextRepository is HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository.
139      In Spring Security 6, the default SecurityContextRepository is DelegatingSecurityContextRepository.
140      To opt into the new Spring Security 6 default, the following configuration can be used:

154      }

 58      - source=spring5

 60    when:
 61      java.referenced:
 62        pattern: org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.web.reactive.function.client.ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction.setClientCredentialsTokenResponseClient
 63        location: METHOD_CALL
 64    description: setClientCredentialsTokenResponseClient(...) method has been deprecated
 65    message: |
 66      In Spring Security 6, the `setClientCredentialsTokenResponseClient(…)` method has been deprecated. 
 67      You should replace it with `ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction(OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager)`.
 68      
 69      The new class `ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction` provides a more flexible and feature-rich way to handle OAuth2 client exchanges. 
 70      Instead of calling the deprecated method, you should create an instance of the new class and use it for your client exchange logic.
 71      
 72      For example, if you had the following configuration:
 73      ```java
 74      @Bean
 75      public ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction oauth2FilterFunction() {
 76        ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction filterFunction =
 77        new ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction();
 78        
 79        // Deprecated in Spring Security 6
 80        filterFunction.setClientCredentialsTokenResponseClient(
 81          new DefaultClientCredentialsTokenResponseClient()
 82        );
 83        
 84        return filterFunction;
 85      }
 86      ```
 87      
 88      This should be refactored to:
 89      ```java
 90      @Bean
 91      public ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction oauth2FilterFunction(ClientRegistrationRepository clientRegistrationRepository) {
 92        OAuth2AuthorizedClientRepository authorizedClientRepository = new AuthenticatedPrincipalOAuth2AuthorizedClientRepository();
 93        
 94        // Configure the provider with the custom token response client
 95        ClientCredentialsOAuth2AuthorizedClientProvider clientCredentialsProvider = new ClientCredentialsOAuth2AuthorizedClientProvider();
 96        clientCredentialsProvider.setAccessTokenResponseClient(new DefaultClientCredentialsTokenResponseClient());
 97        
 98        // Set up the manager
 99        DefaultOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager authorizedClientManager = new DefaultOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager(clientRegistrationRepository, authorizedClientRepository);
100        authorizedClientManager.setAuthorizedClientProvider(new DelegatingOAuth2AuthorizedClientProvider(clientCredentialsProvider));
101        
102        // Use the constructor that takes the manager
103        return new ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction(authorizedClientManager);
104      }
105      ```
106      
107      Ensure that you have the necessary dependencies for `ServletOAuth2AuthorizedClientExchangeFilterFunction` as well as `OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager` in your build configuration.
108      
109      For more details about the new approach, check the Spring Security documentation links provided below.

122    message: |-
123      To migrate a Java application that uses a Sybase database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:
124  
125      * **Choose your Azure target**:
126        * **Azure SQL Database**: The recommended target for Sybase migration, offering a fully managed PaaS service with high compatibility for most Sybase features.
127        * **Azure SQL Managed Instance**: Provides near 100% compatibility with SQL Server and better support for complex Sybase features like stored procedures and triggers.
128        * **SQL Server on Azure VMs**: For maximum compatibility when PaaS migration is not feasible due to specific Sybase dependencies.
129  
130      * **Assess migration complexity**:
131        * Use **SQL Server Migration Assistant (SSMA) for Sybase** to assess database schema compatibility and generate migration reports.
132        * Identify Sybase-specific features that need conversion (e.g., stored procedures, triggers, data types).
133        * Review T-SQL syntax differences and plan for code modifications.
134  
135      * **Migrate** the existing Sybase database:
136        * Use **SSMA for Sybase** to convert database schema and migrate data to Azure SQL Database or SQL Managed Instance.
137        * Utilize **Azure Database Migration Service (DMS)** for online migrations with minimal downtime.
138        * Test migrated database thoroughly, especially stored procedures and complex queries.
139  
140      * Update the application's **database connection** details: Modify the Java application's configuration to point to the newly provisioned Azure SQL service. Update the connection string (JDBC URL), driver class (from Sybase jConnect to SQL Server JDBC driver), hostname, port, username, and password information accordingly.
141  
142      * **Address compatibility issues**:
143        * Replace Sybase-specific SQL syntax with T-SQL equivalents.
144        * Update data type mappings (e.g., Sybase datetime to SQL Server datetime2).
145        * Modify stored procedures and functions to use T-SQL syntax.
146        * Test and update any Sybase-specific driver configurations.
147  
148      * Enable **monitoring and diagnostics**: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying Azure SQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.
149  
150      * Implement **security** measures: Apply security best practices including Azure AD authentication, transparent data encryption, and leverage Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.
151  
152      * **Backup** your data: Azure SQL Database and SQL Managed Instance provide automated backups by default. Configure retention periods and consider geo-redundant backups for enhanced data durability.

 25    - title: How to use JSF 1.2 with EAP 7?
 26      url: https://access.redhat.com/solutions/2773121
 27    message: "\n                        Seam 2.2 and earlier is not supported on JBoss
 28      EAP 6 and above.\n                        Consider migration to Context Dependency
 29      Injection (CDI) standard which covers most of Seam 2 core functionalities in\n
 30      \                       a standardized, type safe and extensible way.\n                        \n
 31      \                       Seam 2.3 still could work on EAP 6.x, but is not maintained
 32      and officially supported on new EAP 6.x patched releases or EAP 7.x.\n\n                        There
 33      are two options available:\n                        \n                        1.
 34      Continue using Seam 2.x on EAP 6 but expect there are bugs or glitches and you
 35      need to fix it yourself.\n                        This approach is sometimes lower
 36      effort but the application will not use a tested and supported library and some
 37      Seam framework features doesn't have to work as expected.\n                        2.
 38      The similar approach as for point 1 but for Seam 2.3 runtime on EAP7 is not verified
 39      and therefore not recommended. Some Seam 2.3 features could work on EAP7,\n                        but
 40      the expected behavior can differ based on what your application uses and how.\n
 41      \                       2. Switch to standard CDI beans and migrate to JSF 2.2
 42      if your server platform is EAP 7+. This will require significant migration effort.\n
 43      \                   "

 988    message: |-
 989      Previous versions of Hibernate have mapped `byte[]` and `Byte[]` to Oracle’s `LONG RAW` data type (via the JDBC `LONGVARBINARY` type). Oracle have deprecated the `LONG RAW` data type for many releases - possibly as far back as 8i.
 990  
 991       Therefore it was decided to start having Hibernate map `byte[]` and `Byte[]` to `BLOB` for Oracle.
 992  
 993       However, in the interest of backwards compatibility and not breaking existing applications it was also decided to limit this change to just the `Oracle12cDialect`. So starting in 5.1 applications using `Oracle12cDialect` and implicitly mapping `byte[]` and `Byte[]` values will start seeing those handled as `BLOB` data rather than `LONG RAW` data.
 994       For existing applications that want to continue to use `Oracle12cDialect` and still continue to implicitly map `byte[]` and `Byte[]` attributes to `LONG RAW`, there is a new configuration setting you can use to enable that: `hibernate.dialect.oracle.prefer_longvarbinary`, which is `false `by default (map to `BLOB`).

 47  
 48       The following is an example of how to send a link header with the RESTEasy client in EAP 6 with RESTEasy 2.3.x.
 49  
 50       ```java
 51       ClientRequest request = new ClientRequest(generateURL("/linkheader/str"));
 52       request.addLink("previous chapter", "previous", "http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2", null);
 53       ClientResponse response = request.post();
 54       LinkHeader header = response.getLinkHeader();
 55       ```
 56  
 57       The following is an example of how to accomplish the same task with the RESTEasy client in RESTEasy 3.
 58  
 59       ```java
 60       ResteasyClient client = new ResteasyClientBuilder().build();
 61       Response response = client.target(generateURL("/linkheader/str")).request()
 62       .header("Link", "<http://example.com/TheBook/chapter2>; rel="previous";
 63       title="previous chapter">").post(Entity.text(new String()));
 64       javax.ws.rs.core.Link link = response.getLink("previous");
 65       ```

 14    message: |-
 15      Sonic ESB services inherit from XQService. In Camel, this can be achieved through the simple Java Bean Camel Component.
 16  
 17       * [Camel Java Bean Component](http://camel.apache.org/bean.html)
 18    ruleID: sonic-esb-01000

 28    description: Reference to com.sonicsw.xq.XQServiceContext
 29    effort: 4
 30    labels:
 31    - source=sonic
 32    - target=fuse6+
 33    - target=fuse
 34    - sonic-esb
 35    - camel
 36    links: []
 37    message: |-
 38      Sonic ESB services leverage the service(XQServiceContext context) method to implement business logic. When messages are routed to the service, the service(XQServiceContext context) method is executed.
 39       In Camel, this is achieved by routing messages to the Java Bean via the Camel Route's Bean Component syntax.
 40  
 41       * [Camel Java Bean Component](http://camel.apache.org/bean.html)
 42       * [Camel Binding Annotations](http://camel.apache.org/parameter-binding-annotations.html)
 43  
 44       Camel's Java Bean Component can leverage annotations annotations on the method to specify how Camel Message body values are mapped to the method parameters. Additionally, the @Handler annotation can be leveraged to setup the default Java Bean method.
 45  
 46       **For example:**
 47  
 48       ```java
 49       public void service(XQServiceContext ctx) throws XQServiceException \{{
 50       ...
 51       }}
 52       ```
 53  
 54       **Should become:**
 55  
 56       ```java
 57       @Handler
 58       public void service(@Header messageHeader, @Body messageBody, Exchange exchange) \{{
 59       ...
 60       }}
 61       ```
 62  
 63       * org.apache.camel.Body
 64       * org.apache.camel.Header
 65       * org.apache.camel.Exchange
 66    ruleID: sonic-esb-02000
 67    when:
 68      or:
 69      - java.referenced:
 70          location: TYPE
 71          pattern: com.sonicsw.xq.XQServiceContext
 72      - java.referenced:

 74          pattern: com.sonicsw.xq.XQServiceContext

644    description: ESB Notifier Action
645    effort: 7
646    labels:
647    - source=soa-p5-
648    - source=soa-p
649    - target=fsw6+
650    - target=fsw
651    - jboss-esb
652    links: []
653    message: |-
654      JBoss ESB uses notifiers to transform ESB aware messages to a format that ESB-unaware services can handle. Fuse Service Works uses bi-directional gateways to transfer messages
655       via its service bindings.
656  
657       A JBoss ESB Notifier should be converted to a Fuse Service Works Service Binding.
658  
659       For example:
660  
661       ```xml
662       <service category="routerToFile" name="FileRouterListener" description="Static route file destination">
663       <actions mep="OneWay">
664       <action name="notificationAction" class="org.jboss.soa.esb.actions.Notifier">
665       <property name="okMethod" value="notifyOK"/>
666       <property name="notification-details">
667       <NotificationList type="ok">
668       <target class="NotifyFiles">
669       <file append="false" URI="/tmp/HelloWorldFileNotifierTest.log"/>
670       </target>
671       </NotificationList>
672       </property>
673       </action>
674       </actions>
675       </service>
676       ```
677  
678  
679       Could be translated to:
680  
681       ```xml
682       <sca:reference name="HelloWorld" multiplicity="0..1" promote="MyComponent/HelloWorld">
683       <camel:binding.file>
684       <camel:directory>/tmp</camel:directory>

 77    message: |-

When set to `false`, updates are sent to the database after each method invocation, but are not committed until the end of the transaction. This allows other processes to access the persisted data while the transaction is waiting to be completed.

Entity Enterprise JavaBeans 157 (EJB) \n

This rule flags entity elements in ejb-jar.xml 158 files.

\n

Entity beans are optional in the EJB 3.2 specification and 159 are not supported on Liberty or Liberty Core. The entity bean API is deprecated 160 in WebSphere Application Server traditional V8.5.5 and V9.0 and might be removed 161 in a later version.

\n

The EJBDeploy tool used to deploy applications 162 with entity beans has also been deprecated and may be removed in the future, either 163 at the same time entity beans are removed or prior.

\n

The Java Persistence 164 API (JPA) is an alternative to using EJB entity beans for new database and other 165 persistence-related operations.

\n

Upgrading entity beans can be difficult, 166 but it can be simplified if your application uses design patterns such as DTO, 167 Session Facade, and DAO.

\n
" 168 ruleID: DetectEJBEntityBeansXML 169 when: 170 builtin.xml: 171 filepaths: 172 - ejb-jar.xml 173 namespaces: {} 174 xpath: //*[local-name()='entity'] 175 - category: mandatory 176 customVariables: [] 177 description: Transaction propagation is not supported for Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB) 178 remote interfaces 179 effort: 1 180 labels: 181 - source=websphere 182 - target=openliberty 183 links: 184 - title: Open Liberty migration rules in Windup 185 url: https://www.ibm.com/docs/wamt?topic=rules-open-liberty-migration-in-windup 186 message: "
\n

Liberty does not support outbound or inbound 187 transaction propagation for EJB remote interfaces. By default, EJB beans are container-managed 188 and use the Required transaction attribute. As a result, existing 189 EJB definitions that do not specify any container-transaction properties 190 are configured by default to use transactions although they are not supported. 191

\n

This rule flags Java code that references the following EJB annotations 192 that indicate the use of remote business or home interfaces:

\n
    \n
  • javax.ejb.Remote
    • 193 \n
  • javax.ejb.RemoteHome
    • \n
\n

This rule also flags 194 the following references in the ejb-jar.xml file:

195 \n
    \n
  • <remote/>
    • \n
  • <business-remote/>
    • 196 \n
\n

The EJB specification requires products that support outbound 197 transaction propagation to still send a null transaction context. This context 198 must be rejected by EJB components that use the Required (default), 199 Mandatory , or Supports transaction attributes. A client 200 with an active global transaction cannot start an EJB bean with default transaction 201 attributes if either the client or server is on Liberty.

\n

To enable 202 the client to start the EJB bean, change the EJB bean to use either the RequiresNew 203 or NotSupported transaction attribute. Although these attributes 204 will allow the EJB bean to start, the transactional work that is done by the EJB 205 bean is not committed as part of the client transactions.

\n

Note that 206 transaction propagation is supported for EJB remote interfaces that are running 207 in the same JVM, however this may only be determined with further investigation 208 of the application behavior.

\n

Make sure remote EJB interfaces are needed

209 \n

Often EJB 2.x beans configure the remote interfaces in ejb-jar.xml even 210 when they are not used. You only need remote interfaces if you have code running 211 across two different JVMs. In WebSphere terms, this is either between two different 212 application servers or between a client application and an application server 213 running in different JVMs. CORBA information, such as an iiop:// 214 provider URL, in an EJB lookup is also an indicator that remote EJB beans are 215 being used.

\n

If you are referencing EJB beans using a remote interface 216 that are running in the same JVM, the Local interface can be used and will perform 217 better. Where possible, change annotations from @Remote to @Local and from @RemoteHome 218 to @LocalHome and test all your code scenarios. Likewise for ejb-jar.xml configuration, 219 remove the <remote/> and <business-remote/> 220 definitions and test all scenarios. While transaction propagation is supported 221 for this scenario, the best practice is to convert to using local interfaces to 222 improve performance and remove the perception that methods can be called externally 223 from the same JVM.

\n

If you really need remote interfaces

\n
Wrap 224 the EJB beans in a web service (JAX-WS)
\n

For those EJB beans that require 225 remote access, best practice is to wrap them in a web service. Refer to Annotating an EJB bean to create a web service for instructions 228 on using WebSphere Application Server Developer Tools for Eclipse to make these 229 code changes. After wrapping the EJB beans in web services, use the web service 230 client to call the EJB web service. After testing, you can remove the EJB remote 231 annotations or configuration.

\n
Handling Transaction Propagation
232 Liberty provides Web Services Atomic Transaction (WS-AT) support which enables 233 distributed global transactions. When your EJB are deployed as web services, WS-AT 234 can be used to manage the transactions. See Web Services Atomic Transaction overview for more information. 237 \n

For more information on related topics, see

\n
    \n

1  - category: optional
  2    customVariables: []
  3    description: Move persistence config to a properties file
  4    effort: 1
  5    labels:
  6    - source=java-ee
  7    - source=jakarta-ee
  8    - target=quarkus
  9    links:
 10    - title: Using Hibernate ORM and Jakarta persistence
 11      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#persistence-xml
 12    message: "It is recommended to move persistence related configuration from an XML
 13      file to a properties one.\n This allows centralization of the configuration in
 14      Quarkus. Check the link for more information.\n \n \n Datasource and persistence
 15      configurations in XML can be substituted with a single centralized properties
 16      file. Here is an example of a translation:\n \n The following datasource configuration:\n
 17      ```\n <datasources xmlns=\"http://www.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema\"\n xmlns:xsi=\"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance\"\n
 18      xsi:schemaLocation=\"http://www.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema http://docs.jboss.org/ironjacamar/schema/datasources_1_0.xsd\">\n
 19      <!-- The datasource is bound into JNDI at this location. We reference\n this in
 20      META-INF/persistence.xml -->\n <datasource jndi-name=\"java:jboss/datasources/TasksJsfQuickstartDS\"\n
 21      pool-name=\"tasks-jsf-quickstart\" enabled=\"true\"\n use-java-context=\"true\">\n
 22      <connection-url>jdbc:h2:mem:tasks-jsf-quickstart;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1</connection-url>\n
 23      <driver>h2</driver>\n <security>\n <user-name>sa</user-name>\n <password>sa</password>\n
 24      </security>\n </datasource>\n </datasources>\n ```\n along with the following
 25      persistence configuration:\n ```\n <persistence version=\"2.1\"\n xmlns=\"http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence\"
 26      xmlns:xsi=\"http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance\"\n xsi:schemaLocation=\"\n
 27      http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence\n http://xmlns.jcp.org/xml/ns/persistence/persistence_2_1.xsd\">\n
 28      <persistence-unit name=\"primary\">\n <!-- We use a different datasource for tests,
 29      so as to not overwrite\n production data. This is an unmanaged data source, backed
 30      by H2, an in memory\n database. Production applications should use a managed datasource.
 31      -->\n <!-- The datasource is deployed as WEB-INF/test-ds.xml,\n you can find it
 32      in the source at src/test/resources/test-ds.xml -->\n <jta-data-source>java:jboss/datasources/TasksJsfQuickstartDS</jta-data-source>\n
 33      <properties>\n <!-- Properties for Hibernate -->\n <property name=\"hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto\"
 34      value=\"create-drop\" />\n <property name=\"hibernate.show_sql\" value=\"false\"
 35      />\n </properties>\n </persistence-unit>\n </persistence>\n ```\n can be translated
 36      to:\n ```\n quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:tasks-jsf-quickstart;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1\n
 37      quarkus.datasource.db-kind=h2\n quarkus.datasource.username=sa\n quarkus.datasource.password=sa\n\n
 38      quarkus.hibernate-orm.database.generation=drop-and-create\n ```"
 39    ruleID: persistence-to-quarkus-00000
 40    when:
 41      or:
 42      - builtin.file:
 43          pattern: persistence\.xml
 44      - builtin.file:
 45          pattern: .*-ds\.xml
 46  - category: potential
 47    customVariables: []
 48    description: '@Produces cannot annotate an EntityManager'
 49    effort: 1
 50    labels:
 51    - source=java-ee
 52    - source=jakarta-ee
 53    - target=quarkus
 54    links:
 55    - title: Using Hibernate ORM and Jakarta persistence
 56      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#persistence-xml
 57    - title: Setting up and configuring Hibernate ORM
 58      url: https://quarkus.io/guides/hibernate-orm#setting-up-and-configuring-hibernate-orm
 59    message: "In JavaEE/JakartaEE, using `@PersistenceContext` was needed in order to
 60      inject a data source. Quarkus, on the other hand,\n will create the bean automatically
 61      just by correctly setting up your datasource, so the `@PersistenceContext` annotation can be removed. \nThis also makes having a `@Produces`
 62      annotation\n on the `EntityManager` illegal in Quarkus.\n \n If you are using
 63      a `@Produces` annotation for your EntityManager, and it is not needed after configuring
 64      your datasource, remove it and `@Inject` the EntityManager.\n Otherwise, if the
 65      producer is still needed, please create a qualification for your produced `EntityManager`,
 66      as well as every injection point for the EM.\n \n For instance, you can create
 67      an `ExtendedContext` qualifier:\n ```\n @Qualifier\n @Target({{ ElementType.TYPE,
 68      ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.PARAMETER }})\n @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)\n
 69      public @interface ExtendedContext {{ ... }}\n ```\n and then inject your entity
 70      managers:\n ```\n @ExtendedContext\n public EntityManager getEm() {{\n return
 71      em;\n }}\n ```"
 72    ruleID: persistence-to-quarkus-00011
 73    when:
 74      and:
 75      - java.referenced:
 76          location: IMPORT
 77          pattern: javax.enterprise.inject.Produces
 78        as: file
 79        ignore: true
 80      - java.referenced:
 81          location: IMPORT
 82          pattern: javax.persistence.EntityManager
 83        from: file

1  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-data-access-00001
  2    category: mandatory
  3    effort: 5
  4    labels:
  5    - source=spring5
  6    - target=spring6+
  7    - source=spring-boot2
  8    - target=spring-boot3+
  9    when:
 10      java.dependency:
 11        name: org.hibernate.hibernate-core
 12        upperbound: 5.5.13.Final
 13    description: Spring 6 must use at least Hibernate 5.6.x
 14    message: |
 15      Due to the Jakarta EE migration, Spring 6 must use at least Hibernate 5.6.x. To make Hibernate 5.6.x compatible with
 16      Jakarta, make sure to also switch your hibernate dependency to the `hibernate-core-jakarta` artifact:
 17      ```
 18      <dependency>
 19          <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
 20          <artifactId>hibernate-core-jakarta</artifactId>
 21          <version>5.6.15.Final</version>
 22      </dependency>
 23      ```
 24      Alternatively, consider migrating to Hibernate ORM 6.1 right away (exclusively based on `jakarta.persistence`,
 25      compatible with EE 9 as well as EE 10) which is the Hibernate version that Spring Boot 3.0 comes with.
 26      
 27      Please check the Hibernate 5.6 migration guide in the links provided.
 28    links:
 29    - title: 'Hibernate 5.5 to 5.6 migration guide'
 30      url: https://github.com/hibernate/hibernate-orm/blob/5.6/migration-guide.adoc
 31    - title: 'Spring 6.0 migration guide'
 32      url: https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-framework/wiki/Spring-Framework-6.0-Release-Notes#removed-apis
 33  
 34  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-data-access-00002
 35    category: mandatory
 36    effort: 1
 37    labels:
 38    - source=spring5
 39    - target=spring6+
 40    - target=hibernate6+
 41    when:
 42      or:
 43      - builtin.filecontent:
 44          filePattern: .*\.properties
 45          pattern: hibernate.bytecode.provider=javassist
 46      - builtin.xml:
 47          namespaces:
 48            s: http://www.hibernate.org/xsd/hibernate-configuration
 49          xpath: "/hibernate-configuration/session-factory/property[@name='hibernate.bytecode.provider' and text()='javassist']" 
 50      - java.referenced:
 51          pattern: org.hibernate.bytecode.javassist*
 52      - builtin.filecontent:
 53          filePattern: .*\.java
 54          pattern: setProperty\(\"hibernate.bytecode.provider\", \"javassist\"\)
 55    description: Javassist no longer supported
 56    message: |
 57      Explicit configuration of `hibernate.bytecode.provider=javassist` has been detected. Javassist is no longer supported by Hibernate 5.6 and later.
 58  
 59      The simplest and recommended solution is to remove this property entirely. Hibernate will automatically use Byte Buddy, which is the current default.
 60    links:
 61    - title: 'Hibernate 5.6 migration guide - Javassist removed'
 62      url: https://github.com/hibernate/hibernate-orm/blob/5.6/migration-guide.adoc#javassist-removed

 64  - ruleID: spring-framework-5.x-to-6.0-data-access-00003
 65    category: potential
 66    effort: 5
 67    labels:
 68    - source=spring5
 69    - target=spring6+
 70    - target=hibernate6+
 71    when:
 72      and:
 73        - or:  # Check for Hibernate annotations or clob fields
 74          - java.referenced:
 75              location: ANNOTATION
 76              pattern: javax.persistence.Lob
 77          - java.referenced:
 78              location: FIELD
 79              pattern: java.sql.Clob
 80        - or:
 81          - builtin.filecontent:
 82              filePattern: .*\.(java|properties|xml)
 83              pattern: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQL81Dialect
 84          - java.dependency:
 85              lowerbound: 0.0.0
 86              name: org.postgresql.postgresql
 87    description: Changes to the DDL type for CLOB
 88    message: |
 89      Using `@Lob` or `java.sql.Clob` with PostgreSQL 8.1 dialect might require DDL type changes for CLOBs.
 90  
 91      Consider reviewing DDL generation for CLOB columns and potential migration to 'oid' type if necessary.
 92  
 93      All PostgreSQL JDBC drivers unfortunately just store the oid it created for a `java.sql.Clob` into the text column. 
 94      Although reading back the value with the CLOB API works, PostgreSQL has no knowledge of the reference to the LOB, 
 95      because the oid is not known to PostgreSQL, leading to data loss when vacuumlo (the utility to clean up unused LOBs) runs. 
 96      To avoid the data loss, it is required to use the oid type so that vacuumlo can see the reference.
 97  
 98      Updating to 5.6.2 does not require any schema or application changes by default, but we highly recommend that you migrate 
 99      existing text columns for LOBs to oid to prevent data loss due to the activity of vacuumlo. 
100    links:
101    - title: 'Hibernate 5.6 migration guide - Changes to the DDL type for CLOB'
102      url: https://github.com/hibernate/hibernate-orm/blob/5.6/migration-guide.adoc#changes-to-the-ddl-type-for-clob-in-postgresql81dialect-and-its-subclasses

421    when:
422      java.referenced:
423        pattern: org.springframework.security.web.authentication.rememberme.TokenBasedRememberMeServices
424        location: IMPORT
425    description: Use SHA-256 in Remember Me
426    message: |
427      The `TokenBasedRememberMeServices` implementation now supports SHA-256 for the Remember Me token and this is the
428      default in Spring Security 6. This change makes the implementation more secure by default since MD5 is already proven
429      to be a weak hashing algorithm and vulnerable against collision attacks and modular differential attacks.
430    
431      The new generated tokens now have the information of which algorithm was used to generate the token and that information
432      is used in order to match it. If the algorithm name is not present, then the matchingAlgorithm property is used to check
433      the token. This allows for a smooth transition from MD5 to SHA-256.
434      
435      To opt into the new Spring Security 6 default to encode the tokens while still being able to decode tokens encoded with MD5,
436      you can set the encodingAlgorithm property to SHA-256 and the matchingAlgorithm property to MD5. See the reference
437      documentation and the API docs for more information.

443        url: https://docs.spring.io/spring-security/reference/5.8/migration/servlet/authentication.html#servlet-opt-in-sha256-rememberme

499            location: ANNOTATION
500    description: Change the order value in @EnableTransactionManagement
501    message: |
502      `@EnableTransactionManagement` and `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity` have the same order value, `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. This means
503      that their order in the Spring AOP Advisor chain relative to each other is undefined.
504    
505      This is often fine since most method security expressions don’t require an open transaction to function correctly;
506      however, historically it was sometimes necessary to ensure one happens before the other by setting their order values.
507      
508      @EnableMethodSecurity does not have an order value since it publishes multiple interceptors. Indeed, it cannot
509      attempt backward-compatibility with @EnableTransactionManagement since it cannot set all the interceptors to be in the same advisor chain location.
510      
511      Instead, the values for the `@EnableMethodSecurity` interceptors are based off of an offset of 0. The `@PreFilter` interceptor
512      has an order of 100; `@PostAuthorize`, 200; and so on.
513  
514      So, if after updating you find that your method security expressions are not working due to not having an open
515      transaction, please change your transaction annotation definition from the following:

523    category: optional

534          location: INHERITANCE
535        as: class

537          pattern: createSecurityExpressionRoot
538          location: METHOD
539          filepaths: "{{class.Filepaths}}"
540        from: class
541    description: Use a Custom @Bean instead of subclassing DefaultMethodSecurityExpressionHandler
542    message: |
543      As a performance optimization, a new method was introduced to `MethodSecurityExpressionHandler` that takes a `Supplier<Authentication>` instead of an `Authentication`.
544      This allows Spring Security to defer the lookup of the `Authentication`, and is taken advantage of automatically when you use `@EnableMethodSecurity` instead of `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`.
545      
546      However, let’s say that your code extends DefaultMethodSecurityExpressionHandler and overrides
547      `createSecurityExpressionRoot(Authentication, MethodInvocation)` to return a custom `SecurityExpressionRoot` instance.
548      This will no longer work because the arrangement that `@EnableMethodSecurity` sets up calls `createEvaluationContext(Supplier<Authentication>, MethodInvocation)` instead.
549      
550      Happily, such a level of customization is often unnecessary. Instead, you can create a custom bean with the authorization methods that you need.
551  
552      For example, let’s say you are wanting a custom evaluation of `@PostAuthorize("hasAuthority('ADMIN')")`. You can create a custom `@Bean` like this one:
553      ```
554      class MyAuthorizer {
555        boolean isAdmin(MethodSecurityExpressionOperations root) {
556          boolean decision = root.hasAuthority("ADMIN");
557          // custom work ...
558          return decision;
559        }
560      }
561      ```
562      and then refer to it in the annotation like so:
563      ```
564      @PreAuthorize("@authz.isAdmin(#root)")

database-reliability-01000.description:
To migrate a Java application that uses a database to Azure, we recommend reviewing your architecture for cloud readiness and resilience. 
The following best practices will help improve reliability and avoid common pitfalls:

* **Review and configure all timeout settings** (e.g., connection, socket, and transaction timeouts) based on real-world load and runtime behavior. Avoid hardcoding fixed values without load testing or telemetry.
* **Avoid infinite or excessively long timeouts.** Instead, favor "fail fast" patterns with proper error handling and retries where appropriate.
* **Lower default transaction timeouts,** especially for frameworks using JTA or other global transaction coordinators, to prevent long blocking under failure or overload conditions.
* **Implement exponential backoff** in client retry logic instead of fixed retry intervals. This helps reduce pressure on the system during partial outages and speeds up recovery by minimizing cascading retry storms.
* **Do not assume the database will always be available.** Cloud environments are inherently distributed and failure-prone. Design your application for transient failures, throttling, and restarts.

Consider re-evaluating assumptions in your database interaction layer to ensure your application behaves reliably under cloud-native environments.
database-reliability-01000.title: Consider database reliability when migrating to Azure

links.title: Understanding timeout properties in the JDBC driver

azure-aws-config-credential-01000.description:
The application contains AWS credential configuration.

 * Migrate credentials to **Azure Key Vault**: Create an Azure Key Vault to securely store your application's credentials and sensitive information. Migrate the AWS credentials to Azure Key Vault, which provides a centralized and highly secure storage solution.

 * **Modify application code**: Update the Java application's code to retrieve the required credentials from Azure Key Vault instead of AWS. Use the appropriate Azure SDK or libraries to integrate with Azure Key Vault and fetch the credentials securely during runtime.

 * Implement **Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) authentication**: If the AWS credentials are used for authentication purposes, consider migrating to Azure AD for user authentication and authorization. Implement Azure AD authentication in your Java application to ensure secure access to Azure resources.
azure-aws-config-credential-01000.title: AWS credential configuration

links.title: Quickstart: Azure Key Vault Secret client library for Java

embedded-cache-15000.description:
The application embeds the Spring Boot Cache library.

An embedded cache library is problematic because state information might not be persisted to a backing service.

Recommendation: Use a cache backing service.
embedded-cache-15000.title: Caching - Spring Boot Cache library

azure-database-microsoft-sql-03000.description:
To migrate a Java application that uses a Microsoft SQL database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

 * Use a managed **Azure SQL**: For that create a managed Azure SQL database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements for performance, storage, and availability.

 * **Migrate** the existing Microsoft SQL database: For that you can use the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) to perform an online migration with minimal downtime.

 * Update the application's **database connection** details: Modify the Java application's configuration to point to the newly provisioned Azure SQL. Update the connection string, hostname, port, username, and password information accordingly.

 * Enable **monitoring and diagnostics**: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying Azure SQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

 * Implement **security** measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the Azure SQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

 * **Backup** your data: Azure SQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
azure-database-microsoft-sql-03000.title: Microsoft SQL database found

links.title: Change automated backup settings for Azure SQL Database

azure-tas-binding-01000.description:
The application has configuration for VMware Tanzu Application Service (TAS) service bindings.
 To migrate a Java application that uses TAS service bindings to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:
 
 * Examine the VCAP_SERVICES variable for configuration settings of external services bound to the application

 * Consider using Service Connector to connect Azure compute services to other backing services. 
 This service configures the network settings and connection information (for example, generating environment variables) between compute services and target backing services in management plane.
azure-tas-binding-01000.title: Tanzu Application Service service bindings

unsecure-network-protocol-00000.description:
Using secured protocols such as HTTPS and SFTP (over HTTP and FTP) should now be the norm as applications are more and more exposed and interconnected. 
This CloudReady patterns looks for unescured URI in the source code or deprecated URI libraries. 
Ideally, URLs should be replaced in your source code by secured protocols HTTPS and SFTP (and ensure the infrastructure implements these protocols for the resources your application calls, uses or references).

azure-database-microsoft-oracle-07000.description:
Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

 * **Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL**: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

 * **Use migration tools**: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

 * **Update database drivers and connection strings**: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

google-gcr-to-azure-acr-01000.description:
The application uses Google Container Registry (gcr.io) or Google Artifact Registry ([location]-docker.pkg.dev) for container images.

**Common patterns detected may include:**
* Container image references in Dockerfiles and docker-compose files
* Kubernetes manifests (Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs, CronJobs, Pods) with GCR images
* Configuration files referencing GCR endpoints

**To migrate to Azure Container Registry (ACR):**
* **Provision Azure Container Registry:**
   * Create an ACR instance: `az acr create --name <registry-name> --resource-group <rg> --sku Standard`
* **Migrate container images:**
   * Import images from GCR: `az acr import --name <acr-name> --source gcr.io/<project>/<image>:<tag> --image <image>:<tag>`
   * Or use docker pull/push: `docker pull gcr.io/<project>/<image>` then `docker push <acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
* **Update image references:**
   * Replace `gcr.io/<project>/<image>` with `<acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
   * Replace `<location>-docker.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo>/<image>` with `<acr-name>.azurecr.io/<image>`
   * Update all Dockerfiles, docker-compose files, Kubernetes manifests, and Helm charts
* **Configure authentication:**
   * **For AKS (recommended):** Enable managed identity integration: `az aks update --name <aks-cluster> --attach-acr <acr-name>`
   * **For other services:** Use Azure managed identities or service principals
   * **For local development:** Use `az acr login --name <acr-name>`
* **Remove GCR-specific tooling:**
   * Replace gcloud docker authentication with Azure CLI or service principals
* **For language packages (if using Artifact Registry for npm/Maven/Python):**
   * Use Azure Artifacts for package management instead of Google Artifact Registry
